title: 3 Days on the Big Island: An Honest First-Timer Itinerary
targetQuery: 3 days on the big island itinerary
intro: Three days on Hawaiʻi Island buys you one side of it. The island covers 4,028 square miles, about 63 percent of the Hawaiian archipelago's combined landmass and more than all the other islands together. Kailua-Kona to Hilo runs roughly two hours each way over a saddle that tops out at 6,632 feet. This plan puts you on the Kona side, gives one full day to Hawaiʻi Volcanoes National Park, and is honest about what gets left out.

sections.h2: How to think about three days
sections.body:
Most first-timers try to circle the island and spend the trip in a rental car. Pick one side and take one long day trip out of it. The Daniel K. Inouye Highway, better known as Saddle Road, is 52.7 miles long, tops out at 6,632 feet between Mauna Kea and Mauna Loa, and is the shortest driving route between Hilo and Kailua-Kona.

Hawaiʻi Volcanoes National Park sits about 95 miles southeast of Kailua-Kona on Highway 11, a 2 to 2.5 hour drive each way, according to the National Park Service. Three days means one anchor day, and for most people that is the volcano. If you would rather spend it on the Kohala beaches or Mauna Kea, that is a fair trade. It is still a trade.

Kona International Airport is just north of Kailua-Kona town. Get the car, buy water and food, and go to the water in the late afternoon rather than starting a drive. Kamakahonu Beach at Kailua Pier is a small protected cove next to the Kamakahonu royal residence, and about as easy as an arrival day gets. There is no lifeguard there.

Kahaluʻu Beach Park, south of town, has a full-time lifeguard and shallow, reef-protected snorkeling. It also carries a hazard flag in our conditions data, so ask the tower about the current through the reef before you swim out. Check today's conditions first either way.

From Kona this is a long day, mostly because of driving. Leave early. Entrance is $30 per private vehicle, credit or debit only, since the park does not accept cash. The park itself is open 24 hours a day, 7 days a week, including holidays.

Kīlauea has been erupting inside Halemaʻumaʻu crater at the summit since December 23, 2024, and as of late July 2026 the USGS alert level is Orange, Watch, with intermittent lava fountaining rather than a steady flow. The eruption area is closed. The Park Service directs viewing to open overlooks along the caldera rim, including Uēkahuna, Kīlauea Overlook at Kūkamāhuākea, Kūpinaʻi Pali and Keanakākoʻi, and warns that parking lots can be full by 10 a.m.

Episodic means it may be doing nothing the day you arrive, so check the USGS Kīlauea update that morning and plan around the rest of the park. The Kīlauea Iki Trail crosses the floor of the crater where the 1959 eruption ponded a lava lake up to 413 feet deep, and Chain of Craters Road runs down the slopes of Kīlauea to the sea. Both hold up with no lava in sight.

sections.h2: Day 3: Kohala sand or a South Kona morning
sections.body:
North gets you the island's widest white-sand beach. Hāpuna Beach is a state recreation area on the Kohala coast with lifeguard service, and it charges non-residents $5 per person plus $10 per vehicle to park. Kaunaʻoa next door is usually calmer but has no lifeguard.

South gets you the better snorkeling. Hōnaunau Bay, called Two Step, sits beside Puʻuhonua o Hōnaunau National Historical Park, which is $20 per private vehicle and also does not accept cash. There is no sand and no lifeguard at Two Step. You step off a lava ledge straight into deep water, which is fine on a flat day and not fine on a swelly one.

sections.h2: Kona or Hilo as a base
sections.body:
Hilo averages 120.39 inches of rain a year across 273 days with measurable precipitation, which makes it the fourth-wettest city in the United States. The Kona side is far drier. That is not a reason to avoid Hilo. It is greener and 30 miles from the volcano, but it is why most short-trip visitors stay on the Kona side.

If the volcano is the entire point of your trip, flip the plan. Fly into Hilo, sleep on that side, and drive 30 miles and about 45 minutes to the park instead of 95 miles and 2 to 2.5 hours.

sections.h2: What does not fit in three days
sections.body:
The Mauna Kea summit road above the 9,200-foot Visitor Information Station is unpaved, rough and quite steep, and the mountain's own guidance is to use 4WD low range to reduce brake failure and overheating on the descent. Check your rental agreement before you build a day around it. Access down Waipiʻo Valley Road is limited to Big Island residents, county-permitted tour operators, and people practicing Native Hawaiian traditional and customary rights.

Papakōlea green sand beach is about 3 miles east of Ka Lae, or South Point, at the far south end of the island, and is legally reachable only on foot over pastureland and eroded, rugged paths. Pololū Valley is at the far north end. Both are worth a morning. Neither is worth what it would cost your three-day driving budget.

keyFacts: Hawaiʻi Island covers 4,028 square miles, about 63 percent of the Hawaiian archipelago's combined landmass.
Hawaiʻi Volcanoes National Park is about 95 miles and 2 to 2.5 hours from Kailua-Kona on Highway 11, and 30 miles and about 45 minutes from Hilo.
Park entrance is $30 per private vehicle, credit or debit only, and the park is open 24 hours a day, 7 days a week.
Kīlauea has been erupting inside Halemaʻumaʻu since December 23, 2024, and was at USGS alert level Orange, Watch, in late July 2026.
The eruption area is closed; the Park Service directs viewing to caldera-rim overlooks including Uēkahuna, Kīlauea Overlook, Kūpinaʻi Pali and Keanakākoʻi.
The Park Service warns that parking lots can be full by 10 a.m.
Hilo averages 120.39 inches of rain across 273 days a year, the fourth-wettest city in the United States.
The Daniel K. Inouye Highway, or Saddle Road, is 52.7 miles long and reaches a maximum elevation of 6,632 feet.

cautions: State Parks posts this warning for Hāpuna: dangerous rip currents and pounding shorebreak during periods of high surf, and waves over 3 feet are for experts, with all others staying out. Hawaiʻi's state ocean safety program notes the average wave height when a spinal cord injury occurs is 3 feet. Check live conditions, swim near the tower, and do not turn your back on the water.
Most Kona and Kaʻū beaches have no lifeguard at all. When you have the choice, pick a lifeguarded beach and ask the tower about the day's current before you get in.

The Park Service warns that hazardous volcanic gasses can endanger sensitive groups, naming those with heart or respiratory issues, infants, children, and pregnant women. Check air quality before and during your visit, and bring eye protection and a dust mask for airborne tephra.
The Park Service tells visitors to stay on marked trails and overlooks, never enter closed or restricted areas, and keep a safe distance from earth cracks, cliff edges, vents and fumaroles.
The volcano is a long drive from Kona, and the crossing tops out at 6,632 feet where weather changes fast. Fill the tank before you start, and do not drive it worn out after dark.

title: 5 Days on the Big Island: The Full-Island Itinerary
targetQuery: 5 days on the big island itinerary
intro: Five days is the first honest length for this island. It is enough to see both sides without living in the car, as long as you split where you sleep. This plan gives three nights to the Kona side and two to the Hilo or Volcano side, crosses the island once on Saddle Road, and reaches Hawaiʻi Volcanoes National Park from 30 miles away instead of 95.

sections.body:
The Daniel K. Inouye Highway, or Saddle Road, is 52.7 miles long and is the shortest driving route between Hilo and Kailua-Kona. Driven once, in the middle of a trip, with your bags in the back, it is a good drive. Driven as a day trip to the volcano and back from Kona, it is hours in the car before you have looked at anything: the Park Service puts Kailua-Kona to the park at about 95 miles and 2 to 2.5 hours each way.

So: three nights on the west side, then move. Sleeping in Hilo or up in Volcano village puts the national park 30 miles and about 45 minutes away and makes an after-dark visit realistic, which is when summit glow shows best.

sections.h2: Days 1–2: Kona and the Kohala coast
sections.body:
Start near the airport and stay close the first afternoon. Kahaluʻu and Laʻaloa, or Magic Sands, both have full-time lifeguards in Kailua-Kona, and both carry hazard flags in our conditions data. North on the Kohala coast, Hāpuna is a state recreation area with lifeguard service that charges non-residents $5 per person plus $10 per vehicle, with Kaunaʻoa and Waialea Bay beside it and no lifeguards at either.

Give one flat morning to Hōnaunau Bay next to Puʻuhonua o Hōnaunau National Historical Park, which is $20 per private vehicle and does not accept cash. Kealakekua Bay just north is a state historical park open 7 a.m. to 8 p.m. with no entrance fee, but all vessels are required to obtain a permit from State Parks before transiting the waters of the bay, and permitted vessels are prohibited from landing at Kaʻawaloa flat or launching from Napoʻopoʻo wharf. Reach the Captain Cook Monument on foot down the steep Kaʻawaloa Trail or with one of the permitted commercial kayak operators.

sections.h2: Day 3: cross the island on Saddle Road
sections.body:
Pack out of Kona in the morning. Highway 190 up toward Waimea, then Route 200, the Daniel K. Inouye Highway, east across the middle of the island. Rental car companies used to prohibit driving it and now allow it, but it still climbs to 6,632 feet between Mauna Kea and Mauna Loa. Fill the tank first.

The Mauna Kea access road turnoff sits near the high point. The Visitor Information Station is at 9,200 feet, is open daily 9 a.m. to 9 p.m., and runs free nightly stargazing programs. That is the stop most people should make.

Down the east side you land in Hilo. If it is raining when you get there, that is not bad luck. Hilo sees measurable precipitation on 273 days a year.

Thirty miles and about 45 minutes from Hilo. Entrance is $30 per private vehicle, credit or debit only, and the park is open 24 hours a day, 7 days a week. Go early, because the Park Service warns parking lots can be full by 10 a.m.

Kīlauea has erupted inside Halemaʻumaʻu at the summit since December 23, 2024, in intermittent fountaining episodes rather than continuously, at USGS alert level Orange, Watch, as of late July 2026. The eruption area itself is closed. Viewing is from open rim overlooks including Uēkahuna, Kīlauea Overlook at Kūkamāhuākea, Kūpinaʻi Pali and Keanakākoʻi. Check the USGS Kīlauea update the morning you go, since there may be no episode running.

A full day also covers the Kīlauea Iki Trail down onto the floor of the crater, where the 1959 eruption ponded a lava lake that reached 413 feet deep, and Chain of Craters Road down the slopes of Kīlauea to the sea. Come back after dark if the vents are glowing.

sections.h2: Day 5: Hilo, waterfalls, and the drive back
sections.body:
ʻAkaka Falls State Park is north of Hilo on the Hāmākua coast, open daily 8:30 a.m. to 5 p.m., $5 per person and $10 per vehicle for non-residents, credit card only. The loop footpath is 0.4 miles with stairs, and the falls plunge 442 feet. Rainbow Falls, in Wailuku River State Park at the edge of town, is 80 feet and roadside, open 7 a.m. to 5:30 p.m. with gates locking at 6, and it also charges non-residents $5 per person plus $10 per vehicle.

For water, Richardson Ocean Park and Carlsmith Beach Park east of Hilo both have full-time lifeguards and calm reef-protected pockets. They are rocky rather than sandy, and honu graze in them. NOAA guidance is to stay at least 10 feet, or 3 meters, away on land and in the water.

Then drive back. Budget roughly two hours to Kona, and more than that if you are flying out the same day.

The Visitor Information Station at 9,200 feet is where most visitors should stop. Above it the road is unpaved, rough and quite steep, 4WD only, and the mountain's guidance is to engage 4WD low, downshift and tap the brakes on the descent to avoid brake failure and overheating. Summit access runs from 30 minutes before sunrise to 30 minutes after sunset, and vehicles must be free of invasive species.

The mountain's own public safety guidance is not to go above the Visitor Information Station if you are pregnant, are under 13 years of age, have high blood pressure or a heart or respiratory condition, or are not feeling well. If you want the summit and do not have a proper 4WD, book a tour operator rather than arguing with a rental contract at 13,000 feet.

Five days does not cover Kaʻū and the far south properly. Punaluʻu black sand beach is on the coastal route if you loop back the long way, but Papakōlea green sand beach is about 3 miles east of Ka Lae, or South Point, is legally accessible only on foot, and the paths there are rugged from erosion and illegal vehicle traffic. It deserves its own morning.

Pololū Valley at the north end is another half day. Access down Waipiʻo Valley Road is limited to Big Island residents, county-permitted tour operators, and people practicing Native Hawaiian traditional and customary rights. Leave these for a return trip rather than shaving hours off the volcano.

keyFacts: The Daniel K. Inouye Highway, or Saddle Road, is 52.7 miles long, tops out at 6,632 feet, and is the shortest route between Hilo and Kailua-Kona.
Hawaiʻi Volcanoes National Park is 30 miles and about 45 minutes from Hilo and about 95 miles and 2 to 2.5 hours from Kailua-Kona; entrance is $30 per private vehicle, credit or debit only.
Kīlauea has erupted inside Halemaʻumaʻu since December 23, 2024, in intermittent fountaining episodes; the eruption area is closed and viewing is from caldera-rim overlooks.
The Maunakea Visitor Information Station sits at 9,200 feet, is open 9 a.m. to 9 p.m. daily, and runs free nightly stargazing programs.
Maunakea guidance says do not ascend above the Visitor Information Station if you are pregnant, under 13, have a heart or respiratory condition, or have been SCUBA diving in the prior 24 hours.
ʻAkaka Falls State Park is open 8:30 a.m. to 5 p.m., charges non-residents $5 per person plus $10 per vehicle by credit card only, and the falls plunge 442 feet.
All vessels must obtain a State Parks permit before transiting Kealakekua Bay, and landing at Kaʻawaloa flat is prohibited.
NOAA guidance is to stay at least 10 feet from sea turtles on land and in the water.

cautions: State Parks warns of dangerous rip currents and pounding shorebreak at Hāpuna during periods of high surf, and says waves over 3 feet are for experts with all others staying out. Hawaiʻi's state ocean safety program says shorebreak is an unpredictable and dangerous condition where waves break directly onshore, and that the average wave height when a spinal cord injury occurs is 3 feet.
Hōnaunau Bay, Kaunaʻoa, Waialea, and most of the Kaʻū coast have no lifeguard. There is nobody watching, and Two Step has a lava-ledge entry into deep water with no sand to retreat to.

The Park Service warns that hazardous volcanic gasses endanger sensitive groups, naming people with heart or respiratory issues, infants, children, and pregnant women. Check air quality before you go and take it seriously.
Saddle Road climbs to 6,632 feet, where weather changes fast. Fill up before you leave either side.

Rapid altitude gain on Mauna Kea brings shortness of breath, headache, nausea, impaired judgment and loss of balance. Do not drive above the Visitor Information Station within 24 hours of SCUBA diving, and do not take children under 13 up there.

title: 1 Day on the Big Island from the Kona or Hilo Cruise Port
targetQuery: one day big island cruise port kona hilo
intro: Ships reach Hawaiʻi Island two different ways, and which one you get decides your whole day. Kailua-Kona has no cruise berth, so ships anchor offshore and tender passengers to Kailua Pier in the middle of town. Hilo has the island's largest harbor, a working commercial port on Hilo Bay with nothing walkable at the gate. One drops you in a walkable town. The other does not.

sections.h2: Kona: you tender, and it costs you hours
sections.body:
The harbor at Kailua-Kona cannot take a cruise ship, so you anchor and ride a tender in. Tendering takes time at both ends of the day, and the queue home is the slower one. Subtract it from your window before you plan anything.

The trade is where you land. Kailua Pier sits in downtown Kailua-Kona, with shops and restaurants within walking distance. Kamakahonu Beach is at the pier itself, a small protected cove beside the Kamakahonu royal residence and Ahuʻena Heiau, with no lifeguard. Mokuʻaikaua Church on Aliʻi Drive is the oldest Christian church in the Hawaiian Islands, with a congregation dating to 1820. If the tender eats your morning, you can still have a real day without a car.

sections.h2: Hilo: you dock, but you are not downtown
sections.body:
Hilo ships tie up in Hilo Harbor, the largest harbor on the island. It is a commercial cargo port with nothing walkable at the gate, and historic downtown is a short drive away. The rental agencies are at Hilo International Airport, which sits right beside the harbor.

What you lose in walkability you gain in reach. Hawaiʻi Volcanoes National Park is 30 miles and about 45 minutes from Hilo, which is the one thing that makes a Hilo port day different from a Kona one.

Entrance is $30 per private vehicle, credit or debit only, and the park is open 24 hours a day, 7 days a week. Kīlauea has been erupting inside Halemaʻumaʻu at the summit since December 23, 2024, in intermittent fountaining episodes rather than continuously, at USGS alert level Orange, Watch, as of late July 2026. The eruption area is closed. Viewing is from open overlooks on the caldera rim, including Uēkahuna, Kīlauea Overlook at Kūkamāhuākea, Kūpinaʻi Pali and Keanakākoʻi, and the Park Service warns those lots can be full by 10 a.m.

Budget about 90 minutes of driving round trip plus at least two hours inside the park, and check the USGS Kīlauea update the morning you dock, because an episode may not be running. If it is not, the Kīlauea Iki Trail across the crater floor and the Crater Rim Drive tour around the summit still justify the drive.

If the park does not fit your window, Rainbow Falls is roadside in Wailuku River State Park at the edge of town, 80 feet high with no hiking, open 7 a.m. to 5:30 p.m. with gates locking at 6, and it charges non-residents $5 per person plus $10 per vehicle. ʻAkaka Falls State Park is north on the Hāmākua coast, open 8:30 a.m. to 5 p.m., $5 per person plus $10 per vehicle for non-residents, credit card only, on a 0.4-mile loop footpath with stairs.

Richardson Ocean Park and Carlsmith Beach Park are east of Hilo and both have full-time lifeguards. They are rocky reef pockets rather than sand beaches, and honu feed in them, so keep at least 10 feet of distance under NOAA guidance.

sections.h2: What a Kona day can actually reach
sections.body:
South of town, Kahaluʻu Beach Park has a full-time lifeguard and shallow reef snorkeling, though it carries a hazard flag in our conditions data for current through the reef. Laʻaloa, or Magic Sands, is also lifeguarded, but the sand strips off it in winter swell, which is how it got the name, and it carries a hazard flag too. North, Hāpuna Beach is a state recreation area on the Kohala coast with lifeguard service and a non-resident fee of $5 per person plus $10 per vehicle.

Kona coffee farms in the hills above town are a shorter option that keeps you close to the pier. Whatever you book, confirm your all-aboard time first.

sections.h2: What will not work from either port
sections.body:
Do not attempt Hawaiʻi Volcanoes National Park from Kona. The Park Service puts it at about 95 miles and 2 to 2.5 hours each way on Highway 11, which is roughly five hours of driving before you have seen anything. The ship will leave without you.

Mauna Kea's summit is out as well. The road above the 9,200-foot Visitor Information Station is unpaved, rough and steep, 4WD only, and summit access closes 30 minutes after sunset. Papakōlea green sand beach is about 3 miles east of Ka Lae, or South Point, at the far southern end of the island and legally reachable only on foot. Access down Waipiʻo Valley Road is limited to residents, county-permitted tour operators, and Native Hawaiian traditional and customary practitioners.

keyFacts: Kailua-Kona has no cruise berth; ships anchor offshore and tender passengers to Kailua Pier in downtown Kailua-Kona.
Hilo Harbor is the largest harbor on the island, and Hilo International Airport, where the rental agencies are, sits beside it.
Hawaiʻi Volcanoes National Park is 30 miles and about 45 minutes from Hilo, but about 95 miles and 2 to 2.5 hours from Kailua-Kona.
Park entrance is $30 per private vehicle, credit or debit only, and the park is open 24 hours a day, 7 days a week.
Kīlauea has erupted inside Halemaʻumaʻu since December 23, 2024, in intermittent episodes; the eruption area is closed and the Park Service warns overlook parking can be full by 10 a.m.
ʻAkaka Falls State Park closes at 5 p.m. and charges non-residents $5 per person plus $10 per vehicle, credit card only.
Rainbow Falls, in Wailuku River State Park, is 80 feet high, open 7 a.m. to 5:30 p.m., and charges non-residents $5 per person plus $10 per vehicle.
The Mauna Kea summit road above the 9,200-foot Visitor Information Station is 4WD only, and summit access ends 30 minutes after sunset.

Hawaiʻi Island has few lifeguarded beaches. Hawaiʻi's state ocean safety program says shorebreak is an unpredictable and dangerous condition where waves break directly onshore, that the average wave height when a spinal cord injury occurs is 3 feet, and that you should avoid going into the water at beaches with dangerous shorebreak.

The Park Service warns that hazardous volcanic gasses endanger sensitive groups, naming people with heart or respiratory issues, infants, children, and pregnant women. Check air quality before you drive up.
The Park Service tells visitors to stay on marked trails and overlooks, never enter closed or restricted areas, and keep a safe distance from earth cracks, cliff edges, vents and fumaroles.
Do not try the national park from Kona on a port day. About five hours of round-trip driving against a fixed departure is how people get left behind.

title: The Best Time to Visit the Big Island: Season by Season
targetQuery: best time to visit big island hawaii
intro: The Big Island runs two weather calendars at once, so the right month depends on which coast you will be standing on. The Hilo side averages 120 to 127 inches of rain a year and has no dry month. The leeward shoreline gauges near Kailua Kona and Kawaihae average under ten. Whales, swell and hurricane season each have their own window. Here is what the year actually looks like, coast by coast.

sections.body:
There is no single best month, because the island does not have one season. It has a windward season and a leeward season running at the same time. On the east side, Hilo's driest month is June at about 7.4 inches and its wettest is November at about 15.5 inches, out of an annual total of roughly 120 to 127 inches depending on the gauge. On the leeward shoreline, the 1991-2020 normals for the Kailua Kona gauge and the Puʻukoholā Heiau gauge near Kawaihae are 9.9 and 9.0 inches for the entire year.

So pick by what you came for. Humpback whales are in Hawaiian waters November through April. North Pacific swell lands on the north and west facing shores in the state's winter season, November through April. Southern Hemisphere swell reaches the south facing Kaʻū coast in the summer season, May through October. Central Pacific hurricane season runs June 1 to November 30. The month-by-month weather guide breaks the numbers down by side.

Humpback whales are in Hawaiian waters November through April, and the sheltered Kona and Kohala coasts on the west side are the easiest place to look for them from shore.

Winter is also the state's high-surf season for north and west facing shores. Hāpuna, Kaunaʻoa, Kua Bay and Pololū are the beaches that change most. Hilo is wet in these months: about 9.3 inches in January, 9.6 in February and 13.4 in March. Kona is at its driest, with February averaging about 1.6 inches, and December and January are its least cloudy months at under 50 percent cover.

Trade winds are least dependable now, blowing 50 to 80 percent of the time from October through April against 80 to 95 percent from May through September. Snowstorms drop a foot or more on the upper slopes of Mauna Kea and Mauna Loa several times a year on average, almost always between October and May.

The last whales trail off through April. Hilo is still wet in April at about 11.5 inches, then drops to about 8.1 in May. On the Kona side the trend runs the other way: April through June are the cloudiest months of the year there, at roughly 70 percent cloud cover, as the afternoon shower cycle sets in.

One scheduling note for the east side. The Merrie Monarch Festival is a week-long hula festival in Hilo; the 2026 festival ran April 5 to 11 and the 2027 festival is scheduled for March 28 to April 3. If you want to be in Hilo that week, book well ahead.

Summer flips the Kona coast. Unlike the rest of the state, the leeward Kona side is wetter in summer than in winter: at Nāpoʻopoʻo the average monthly rainfall is 2.80 inches in winter against 3.70 in summer. In Kailua-Kona the wettest months are July and September at about 2.9 inches each, which is still less than Hilo's driest month.

Mornings are the usable part on that coast. Kona skies are clearest from 8 to 10 a.m. and reach roughly 80 percent cloud cover by 2 p.m. Meanwhile Hilo has its driest month in June at about 7.4 inches, then climbs back to about 10.8 in July.

The south facing Kaʻū coast, including Punaluʻu and the Honuʻapo area, gets its surf now: the state lists large swells arriving frequently on south shores in the May through October season. Central Pacific hurricane season runs June 1 to November 30, and NOAA's 2026 outlook gave a 70 percent chance of an above-normal season with 5 to 13 tropical cyclones. That is a seasonal probability, not a forecast of anything hitting the island.

October still reads like summer on the east side, with Hilo highs near 83°F and about 9.8 inches of rain. The exception on the west side is Ironman week. The 2026 Ironman World Championship returns to Kailua-Kona with the men's and women's races on the same day, scheduled for Saturday, October 10. The town is busy for days around it.

November is the wettest month in Hilo, averaging about 15.5 inches. On the leeward side it is one of the two driest months at about 1.7 inches. November is also when humpback whales start arriving in Hawaiian waters.

sections.h2: The things that do not follow a season
sections.body:
Kīlauea has been intermittently active within Halemaʻumaʻu crater at the summit since December 23, 2024, in lava fountaining episodes that have mostly continued for a day or less. Whether you see lava is not a matter of picking the right month. Check the USGS Hawaiian Volcano Observatory updates a day or two before you go, and check the park's own alerts.

Vog is the other one. It is the hazy air pollution caused by volcanic emissions from Kīlauea, and under trade winds the far downwind area is primarily the west side of Hawaiʻi Island, while communities closer to the vents, from Ocean View to Hilo, get both sulfur dioxide gas and fine particles. The park warns that hazardous volcanic gases can be a danger to sensitive groups and tells visitors to check air quality frequently during a visit.

Hawaiʻi Volcanoes National Park is open 24 hours a day, 7 days a week, including holidays, though the Kahuku Unit is open only Thursday through Sunday, 8 a.m. to 4 p.m. Entry is $30 per vehicle for seven days, $25 per motorcycle, $15 per person on foot or bike, and the park does not accept cash. Remaining 2026 fee-free days are August 25, September 17, October 27 and November 11. Expect closures and delays from a two-year construction project repairing damaged buildings and infrastructure at the summit.

Match the month to the coast you care about. Whales and north-shore surf mean November through April on the Kohala and Kona side. South swell on the Kaʻū coast means May through October. If Hilo, Puna and the volcano are the trip, June is the driest month over there at about 7.4 inches and November is the wettest at about 15.5.

Then check the day itself rather than the season. Conditions on this island change by coast and by hour. Start with today's beach conditions and the surf-season guide so you are on the coast that is out of season for swell.

keyFacts: Hilo averages roughly 120 to 127 inches of rain a year and has no dry month; November is its wettest at about 15.5 inches and June its driest at about 7.4.
In the 1991-2020 normals the leeward shoreline gauges read 9.9 inches a year at Kailua Kona and 9.0 inches at Puʻukoholā Heiau near Kawaihae.
Humpback whales are in Hawaiian waters November through April.
Kailua-Kona's wettest months are July and September at about 2.9 inches each, and its driest are February at about 1.6 and November at about 1.7.
Central Pacific hurricane season runs June 1 to November 30; NOAA's 2026 outlook gave a 70 percent chance of an above-normal season with 5 to 13 tropical cyclones.
The 2026 Ironman World Championship is in Kailua-Kona on Saturday, October 10, with the men's and women's races on the same day.
The Merrie Monarch Festival is a week-long hula festival in Hilo; the 2027 festival is scheduled for March 28 to April 3.
Hawaiʻi Volcanoes National Park charges $30 per vehicle for seven days, is open 24 hours a day year-round, and does not accept cash.

cautions: The state lists north shores as getting consistent huge and dangerous swells from November through April, and west shores as taking wrapped north swell in both seasons. The state parks warning for Hāpuna is blunt: dangerous rip currents and pounding shore breaks during periods of high surf, and waves over 3 feet high are for experts only.

Never dive headfirst into shorebreak. The state's ocean safety guidance says the average wave height when spinal cord injuries occur is just 3 feet, and tells swimmers to duck under oncoming waves instead.
Hawaiʻi Island has ten lifeguarded beaches and they are staffed 9:30 a.m. to 4:45 p.m., seven days a week. Outside those hours and beaches nobody is watching the water.

The Maunakea summit road above the Visitor Information Station is four-wheel-drive only, the summit is open only from 30 minutes before sunrise to 30 minutes after sunset, and vehicles must be clean and free of invasive species. Major storms drop a foot or more of snow on the upper slopes several times a year, almost always October through May.

Under trade winds vog drifts primarily onto the west side of Hawaiʻi Island, and communities from Ocean View to Hilo get both sulfur dioxide gas and fine particles. The national park tells visitors to check air quality frequently, and warns that volcanic gases can be dangerous to sensitive groups.

title: Big Island Weather Month by Month: What to Actually Expect
intro: The Big Island is not one climate. Hilo's gauges read 120 to 127 inches of rain a year. The leeward shoreline gauges at Kailua Kona and Puʻukoholā Heiau near Kawaihae read under ten in the same 1991 to 2020 normals. A statewide forecast tells you almost nothing about the beach you are standing on, and the wettest and driest months are not the same on the two coasts. Here is the month-by-month read, side by side.

sections.body:
Trade winds prevail 80 to 95 percent of the time from May through September and 50 to 80 percent from October through April. Where those winds hit the windward slopes, they make rain. Hilo and the Hāmākua and Puna coasts sit in that band and are wetter than anywhere else in the state.

The Kona coast does the opposite. It sits in the lee of Mauna Loa and Hualālai, and its summers are wetter than its winters. At Nāpoʻopoʻo the average monthly rainfall is 2.80 inches in winter against 3.70 in summer. That is the reverse of the usual Hawaiian pattern, and the rain there has a reliable time of day.

Hilo highs sit at 79°F with lows of 64 to 65. Rainfall runs about 9.3 inches in January, 9.6 in February and 13.4 in March. Kailua-Kona's coolest month is January, averaging about 71°F, and February is its driest month at roughly 1.6 inches. December and January are Kona's least cloudy months, at under 50 percent cover against an annual average of 57.

This is also when trade winds are least dependable, blowing 50 to 80 percent of the time from October through April. Major storms deposit a foot or more of snow on the upper slopes of Mauna Kea and Mauna Loa several times a year on average, almost always between October and May.

April is still wet in Hilo at about 11.5 inches, then May drops to about 8.1 and June to about 7.4. June is Hilo's driest month, which is worth knowing if the volcano and the east side are the point of your trip.

On the Kona side the trend runs the other way. April through June are the cloudiest months there, at roughly 70 percent cover, as the afternoon shower cycle sets in. Water temperature off Hilo climbs from its March low of about 75°F to about 78 by June.

These are the warmest months. Hilo highs reach 83°F with lows of 69 to 70. Kailua-Kona's warmest month is August at about 78°F. Kona's wettest months are July and September at about 2.9 inches each, still less than Hilo's driest month; Hilo itself runs about 10.8 inches in July, 9.9 in August and 9.9 in September.

The daily rhythm matters more than the monthly total on the leeward side. Kona skies are clearest from 8 to 10 a.m. and reach roughly 80 percent cloud cover by 2 p.m. Water temperature off Hilo peaks at about 80°F in September. Central Pacific hurricane season runs in the background from June 1 to November 30.

October holds summer's warmth on the east side, with Hilo highs still near 83°F and about 9.8 inches of rain. Then the windward side turns: November is Hilo's wettest month at about 15.5 inches, with December around 11.6. Fifteen inches in a month is real rain.

Kona goes the other way. November is one of its two driest months at about 1.7 inches, and December and January are its least cloudy at under 50 percent cover. Humpback whales start arriving in Hawaiian waters in November.

Coastal numbers do not apply once you go up. The Kīlauea summit area sits at roughly 4,000 feet, and the National Park Service says the weather there varies daily and may be rainy and chilly any time of year, running 12 to 15 degrees cooler than at sea level. Volcano Village sits in that same band, which is why people show up in beach clothes and regret it. Waimea, also well upslope on the north side, is likewise cooler than the coast below it.

The summits are another matter again. At high elevation the relative humidity is generally below 40 percent and often falls to 10 or even 5 percent; the Mauna Loa Observatory gauge averages just 14.3 inches of rain a year. Snow falls on the upper slopes several times a year, almost always between October and May.

sections.h2: The two things that ruin a Big Island day
sections.body:
The first is vog, the hazy air pollution caused by volcanic emissions from Kīlauea. Under trade winds the far downwind area is primarily the west side of Hawaiʻi Island, which gets mostly fine particles, while communities closer to the vents, from Ocean View to Hilo, get both sulfur dioxide gas and fine particles. The national park warns that hazardous volcanic gases can be a danger to sensitive groups and tells visitors to check air quality frequently.

The second is runoff. The Department of Health warns that after any storm event, storm water runoff may contain sewage, harmful micro-organisms and chemicals, and that the public should stay out of beaches or streams contaminated by brown water. Coastal water typically clears within about 48 hours through tidal flushing, but the guidance is to wait for further instructions from the Department of Health rather than to guess. Check live conditions before you get in.

keyFacts: Hilo's monthly rainfall runs from about 7.4 inches in June to about 15.5 inches in November, with highs of 79 to 83°F and lows of 64 to 70°F.
Hilo's annual rainfall reads between 120.4 and 126.7 inches depending on the gauge, both from 1991-2020 normals.
The 1991-2020 shoreline normals are 9.9 inches a year at Kailua Kona and 9.0 at Puʻukoholā Heiau near Kawaihae, while gauges in Kailua-Kona town total about 27 inches.
The Kona coast's summers are wetter than its winters: 2.80 inches a month in winter at Nāpoʻopoʻo against 3.70 in summer.
Kona skies are clearest from 8 to 10 a.m. and reach roughly 80 percent cloud cover by 2 p.m.
Trade winds prevail 80 to 95 percent of the time May through September and 50 to 80 percent October through April.
Water temperature off Hilo runs from about 75°F in March to about 80°F in September.
Major storms drop a foot or more of snow on the upper slopes of Mauna Kea and Mauna Loa several times a year, almost always between October and May.

The state lists north shores as getting consistent huge and dangerous swells November through April and south shores as getting large swells frequently May through October, on days that can look clear and pleasant. Check the forecast for that specific shore before you get in.

After a storm, storm water runoff can carry sewage, harmful micro-organisms and chemicals into the ocean. Stay out of brown or murky water and out of contaminated streams, and wait for the Department of Health rather than judging by eye.

Do not swim or wade in any freshwater stream or pond in Hawaiʻi. The Department of Health warns of leptospirosis, especially with open cuts or sores, and notes that putting your head underwater raises the risk of infection through the eyes, nose and mouth.

The Maunakea summit road above the Visitor Information Station is four-wheel-drive only and the summit is open only from 30 minutes before sunrise to 30 minutes after sunset. Humidity at that elevation is generally below 40 percent and can fall to 5, and snow falls on the upper slopes from October through May.
Averages are not promises. Any month here can deliver a week of rain on the coast you chose, so keep at least one flexible day and be willing to drive to the other side.

title: Big Island Surf Season: When Each Shore Is Calm (and When It Is Not)
targetQuery: big island surf season by shore
intro: The Big Island has four coasts and they are never all calm at once. The state's ocean safety guidance splits the year into a summer season from May through October and a winter season from November through April, and each shore direction behaves differently in each. Picking the coast that is out of season for swell matters more than picking the beach. Here is how each shore reads through the year.

sections.h2: Winter: the north and west shores take the hits
sections.body:
For the winter season, November through April, the state describes north shores as getting consistent huge and dangerous swells, and says inexperienced surfers and swimmers of any skill level should avoid entering the water at those beaches during high-surf conditions. On this island the north-facing shore is Pololū Valley. West shores get north swell wrapping around to create high surf, and the state lists that in both seasons, so the Kohala and Kona strip is never fully out of season: Hāpuna, Kaunaʻoa, Waialea, Mauʻumae, Spencer, Kīholo, Kua Bay, Makalawena and Mahaiʻula all face roughly west.

Hāpuna is the one that catches visitors out. It is a wide white-sand beach with a lifeguard, and the state parks warning for it is direct: dangerous rip currents and pounding shore breaks during periods of high surf, and waves over 3 feet high are for experts, with all others to stay out of the water. Check Hāpuna conditions and Kua Bay conditions before you commit to a beach day up there.

sections.h2: Summer: the Kaʻū south coast turns on
sections.body:
In the summer season, May through October, the state says large swells can arrive frequently on south shores; in winter it lists those same shores as flat-to-small. On the Big Island that means the Kaʻū coast: Punaluʻu, Whittington and Honuʻapo, Kaʻalualu, Papakōlea and Ka Lae. The more southwest-facing Kona spots pick up the same swell, and Kahaluʻu faces south-southwest.

This coast has almost no lifeguard coverage. Punaluʻu is the only beach in Kaʻū on the state's lifeguarded list. Papakōlea, Ka Lae, Kaʻalualu and Whittington are not on it, and they have no shade and long walks or rough tracks between you and help.

sections.h2: The Hilo and Puna side is a trade-wind coast year round
sections.body:
The east side does not have an off-season. The state's ocean safety guidance uses identical wording for east shores in both the summer and the winter season: strong trade winds can create large, rough waves. That is an honest way of saying the exposure never really goes away, and it lines up with trade winds prevailing 80 to 95 percent of the time in summer and 50 to 80 percent in winter.

Honoliʻi, an east-northeast facing rivermouth break north of Hilo, is one of the island's best-known surf spots and is at its best in winter. Pohoiki and Kehena in Puna face south-southeast and pick up both trade swell and summer south swell. The Hilo bayfront parks, Richardson, Carlsmith, Leleiwi and Onekahakaha, sit behind reef and rock and are the more protected end of that coast, but protected is not calm.

sections.h2: Where it is protected by geography rather than by season
sections.body:
A few spots owe their shelter to shape rather than the calendar. Kamakahonu, the small beach behind Kailua Pier in Kailua-Kona, sits inside the pier and is one of the more sheltered pockets of water on the west side. Onekahakaha in Hilo has a rock-walled shallow pond and is one of the ten lifeguarded beaches on the island. Hōnaunau Bay, the Two Step entry, has no sand at all: you get in and out over a bare lava ledge, there is no lifeguard, and a real swell makes the exit difficult.

Kahaluʻu deserves a specific warning. A breakwater reef takes much of the wave energy, and nearly half a million people visit each year, which makes it one of the most popular snorkel spots on the island and one with a full-time lifeguard. The Kahaluʻu Bay Education Center still tells people to enter and exit through the channel in front of the lifeguard tower and warns that large waves, strong currents, sharp rocks and sea urchins are common and that conditions in the bay can change rapidly. It also asks visitors to wait for the lifeguards before entering the water.

sections.h2: Mornings beat afternoons on the Kona side
sections.body:
The leeward coast runs on a land and sea breeze cycle rather than steady trades. Kona skies are clearest from 8 to 10 a.m. and reach roughly 80 percent cloud cover by 2 p.m., and the leeward side's rain is an afternoon pattern rather than an all-day one.

That is the practical reason the west-side boats leave early. If you want the calmest, clearest part of the Kona day, be in the water in the morning and treat the afternoon as land time.

sections.h2: How to read a day here
sections.body:
Check the forecast for the shore you are going to, not for the island. A north swell means nothing to Punaluʻu and a great deal to Hāpuna. Then watch the actual water for a full ten minutes before you get in, and count the waves in a set so you see the big ones rather than the average ones.

Hawaiʻi Island has ten lifeguarded beaches, all staffed 9:30 a.m. to 4:45 p.m., Monday through Sunday: Hāpuna, Spencer, Kahaluʻu and White Sands (Laʻaloa) on the west side, and Punaluʻu, Honoliʻi, Richardson, Carlsmith, Leleiwi and Onekahakaha on the east and south. Everything else, including Kua Bay, Makalawena, Papakōlea, Pololū and Two Step, is not on that list. If you are unsure, pick a coast that is out of season for swell and a beach where somebody is on the tower. Start with today's conditions.

keyFacts: The state's ocean safety guidance runs a summer season from May through October and a winter season from November through April.
North shores, including Pololū, get consistent huge and dangerous swells in the November through April winter season.
West shores including Hāpuna, Kaunaʻoa, Kua Bay and Makalawena are listed as taking wrapped north swell in both seasons, so the Kohala and Kona coast has no fully calm season.
South shores including Punaluʻu, Honuʻapo, Ka Lae and Papakōlea get large swells frequently from May through October and are flat-to-small in winter.
The state uses the same wording for east shores in both seasons: strong trade winds can create large, rough waves.
The state parks warning for Hāpuna is that waves over 3 feet high are for experts and all others should stay out of the water.
Hawaiʻi Island has exactly ten lifeguarded beaches on the state's list, all staffed 9:30 a.m. to 4:45 p.m., seven days a week.
Kona skies are clearest between 8 and 10 a.m. and reach about 80 percent cloud cover by 2 p.m.

cautions: Never dive into shorebreak head first. The state's guidance says this can drive you into the ocean floor and cause serious injury to the head, neck and spinal cord, that the average wave height when spinal cord injuries occur is just 3 feet, and that you should duck under oncoming waves instead.
At Hāpuna, state parks warns of dangerous rip currents and pounding shore breaks during high surf, and says waves over 3 feet high are for experts and everyone else should stay out of the water.

At Kahaluʻu, enter and exit only through the channel in front of the lifeguard tower. Large waves, strong currents, sharp rocks and sea urchins are common, conditions in the bay change rapidly, and the guidance is to wait for the lifeguards before entering the water.

Ka Lae, Papakōlea, Kaʻalualu and Whittington on the Kaʻū coast are not on the state's lifeguarded list. There is no shade and a long way to any help. Do not enter the water there because other people are.

Outside 9:30 a.m. to 4:45 p.m., and at every beach not on the state lifeguard list, nobody is watching the water. A shore that was flat yesterday can have dangerous surf today when a new swell fills in, so check the forecast for that specific shore every time.

title: Mauna Kea: Summit Access, Stargazing, and What to Bring
targetQuery: mauna kea summit stargazing visitor information
intro: Mauna Kea's summit is 13,803 feet, and the paved road ends well below it at the Maunakea Visitor Information Station, 9,200 feet up. Above the station the road is unpaved and four-wheel-drive only, and the mountain's own guidance tells drivers to check whether their rental company allows it. The summit area closes 30 minutes after sunset, so evening stargazing happens lower down. Here is how access, altitude, and weather work on this mountain.

sections.h2: Two different trips: the station and the summit
sections.body:
The Maunakea Visitor Information Station sits at 9,200 feet on the Maunakea Access Road, at Milepost 28 off the Daniel K. Inouye Highway (Saddle Road). It is open 9 a.m. to 9 p.m., 365 days a year, and there is no registration, entrance, or parking fee. Restrooms are outside at the back of the building, and bathroom hours are subject to change based on daily water usage. Food is limited to small snacks for purchase when available, and water is the only drink sold.

The pavement ends about 300 yards past the station. Above that, the eight-mile summit road rises nearly 5,000 feet. Going higher is a separate decision with separate requirements. Driving to the station, watching the sun set from Puʻukalepeamoa, and staying for the stars is a full evening on its own.

sections.h2: Getting above the Visitor Information Station
sections.body:
Two-wheel-drive vehicles are not permitted above the station. A dependable, fully operable 4WD or AWD vehicle is required. Past the end of the pavement, the next four and a half miles are a steep graded-gravel road, and unpaved sections are only wide enough for single-lane traffic. Listed road hazards include atmospheric and solar glare, blind curves, rock debris, and poor traction. On the descent the instruction is to engage 4WD low range, downshift, and tap the brakes, specifically to avoid brake overheating and failure.

Read your rental agreement. The Maunakea visitor site tells drivers to check with their rental car company to see whether they are allowed to travel on Maunakea. Visibly dirty or muddy vehicles will be turned away, and vehicles and gear are supposed to be clean to avoid spreading invasive species.

You are responsible for your own safety on the mountain, and emergency assistance may be hours away. Park only in clearly marked areas or as directed by a Ranger. Minors must be accompanied by an adult at all times. There are no shuttles to the summit; permitted commercial tour services all start from Kona or Hilo and must be prearranged in town.

Acclimate at the station for at least 30 minutes before going higher. At 14,000 feet there is 40 percent less oxygen available than at sea level. The safety guidance lists the signs of altitude sickness as thirst, shortness of breath, headache, nausea, impaired judgment, fatigue or drowsiness, and loss of balance and muscle coordination. Descend immediately and seek medical attention if any of them appear. Altitude sickness can lead to high altitude pulmonary edema and high altitude cerebral edema, which are life-threatening.

Do not travel above the station if you are under 13, are pregnant, are intoxicated, have been scuba diving in the prior 24 hours, or have high blood pressure or a heart or respiratory condition. Anyone in poor health should consult a physician before planning a visit. The scuba rule rules out the combination of a morning dive on the Kona coast and an afternoon drive up the mountain on the same day.

The summit area is closed to visitors from 30 minutes after sunset to 30 minutes before sunrise. There is no public stargazing at the top. Visitors may remain on Maunakea after dark to stargaze, but must descend to Park 2 or below to do it.

There are no formal nighttime programs at the station. After twilight ends, staff step outside and give a laser-guided presentation. Topics vary with staff and time of year and can cover Greek constellations, Hawaiian starlines, wayfinding, notable objects and discoveries in space, and astrophotography. This is weather and staff dependent.

There are no public-use telescopes at the station in the evening. The nightly telescope program was halted in 2019 because of safety concerns and overcrowding that was causing environmental damage. A free once-a-month telescope event now runs instead, with limited capacity and a required reservation.

The lower site is not a worse view. The visitor site states that the lack of oxygen on the summit means your vision is not as acute there, and that you can actually see more stars from the station than from the summit.

sections.h2: Weather and when to turn around
sections.body:
The mountain's safety guidance states that winter conditions may occur at any time, causing freezing temperatures, 100-plus mph winds, and zero-visibility whiteouts. Ice on the ground and falling ice from observatories and other structures are both listed hazards. Snow play is at your own risk, and snowmobiles and devices lacking directional or braking mechanisms, such as inner tubes and boogie boards, are prohibited.

Check road and weather status before you leave the coast. The Maunakea weather hotline is an automated line at (808) 935-6268, and current road and weather information is posted on the visitor site. Obey all road and area closures. If you become stuck in a severe winter storm, stay in your vehicle and turn the engine off to avoid carbon monoxide poisoning.

There are no public gas stations in the area. The stations in Hilo, Waikoloa Village, and Waimea are each about 35 miles away, and the recommendation is at least half a tank before proceeding to the summit. Maunakea has no public accommodations, and most observatory buildings are not open to the public. Camping and overnight sleeping are prohibited, as are fires, including those contained in grills or portable stoves. Drones are prohibited. Pets are not allowed except service animals and hunting dogs.

Cell-phone service is spotty and absent in places. Above the Visitor Information Station, radio, cellphone, Bluetooth, and Wi-Fi use is restricted to emergencies because of interference with the radio telescopes. A public emergency telephone is located at the University of Hawaiʻi 2.2 meter Telescope. Download maps and directions before you drive up. The Maunakea Rangers' line for minor emergencies on the mountain is (808) 960-2952, the station is (808) 934-4550, and 911 is for major emergencies.

Bring cold-weather clothing. Hypothermia and intense solar radiation are both listed hazards, with guidance to use adequate cold-weather clothing, limit your exposure to the cold, and protect yourself with appropriate clothing, sunscreen, and sunglasses. The summit air is extremely dry, and the suggested intake is about 16.9 fluid ounces (500 ml) per person per hour. The packing guide covers the rest.

keyFacts: Mauna Kea's summit is 13,803 feet; the Maunakea Visitor Information Station sits at 9,200 feet.
The station is open 9 a.m. to 9 p.m., 365 days a year, with no registration, entrance, or parking fee.
Two-wheel-drive vehicles are not permitted above the station, and the eight-mile summit road rises nearly 5,000 feet.
The summit area is closed to visitors from 30 minutes after sunset to 30 minutes before sunrise; stargazers must descend to Park 2 or below.
Visitors are asked to acclimate at the station for at least 30 minutes before driving higher.
Do not go above the station if you are under 13, pregnant, intoxicated, have scuba dived in the prior 24 hours, or have high blood pressure or a heart or respiratory condition.
The nightly public telescope program was halted in 2019; a free once-a-month telescope event now runs with limited capacity and a required reservation.
The nearest gas stations are in Hilo, Waikoloa Village, and Waimea, each about 35 miles away.

cautions: Do not travel above the Visitor Information Station if you have been scuba diving in the prior 24 hours. A morning dive on the Kona coast rules out the summit that day.
Descend in 4WD low range, downshifting and tapping the brakes. The official instruction exists to avoid brake overheating and failure on four and a half miles of steep graded gravel.
Impaired judgment and loss of balance are listed signs of altitude sickness. If anyone in the vehicle has a headache, nausea, or trouble balancing, descend immediately and seek medical attention.

Winter conditions may occur at any time of year, causing freezing temperatures, 100-plus mph winds, and zero-visibility whiteouts. Call the weather hotline at (808) 935-6268 before leaving the coast and obey all road and area closures.

If you pair a summit day with a beach day, treat the ocean on its own terms. Big Island shore conditions change through the day and many beaches have no lifeguard. Check live conditions before you swim and stay out when waves are breaking onto rock.

title: Vog on the Big Island: What It Is and How to Plan Around It
intro: Vog is the haze that forms when sulfur dioxide from an erupting volcano reacts in the air and drifts downwind as sulfate aerosol. Kīlauea has been erupting episodically at Halemaʻumaʻu since December 23, 2024, and between fountaining episodes the summit still releases roughly 1,000 to 5,000 tonnes of sulfur dioxide a day. For most visitors this is a flattened view and a scratchy throat. For sensitive groups it is a health issue. It is predictable enough to plan around.

sections.body:
Vog is a hazy mixture of sulfur dioxide gas and aerosols, which are primarily sulfuric acid and other sulfate compounds. The aerosols form when volcanic gases interact chemically with oxygen, moisture, dust, and sunlight over minutes to days. Far from the vents, aerosols are the main component of vog; closer to the volcano it contains both aerosols and unreacted sulfur dioxide gas.

Kīlauea has been erupting episodically since December 23, 2024, from two vents in Halemaʻumaʻu, and more than fifty fountaining episodes have occurred. Episodes generally last less than 12 hours and are separated by pauses that can be longer than three weeks. Between episodes, the summit sulfur dioxide emission rate typically varies within a range of 1,000 to 5,000 tonnes per day, and emissions can remain locally hazardous immediately downwind of the vents even when the vents are not actively erupting.

sections.h2: Where it goes, and why Kona gets it
sections.body:
The main wind direction in the Hawaiian Islands is from the northeast. From May through September the trade winds blow 80 to 95 percent of the time. Under trade wind conditions, vog travels around the southern part of the island and along the Kona coast, where it becomes trapped by daytime onshore and nighttime offshore sea breezes. The leeward side people book for the sunshine is the side that collects the haze.

When trade winds are absent, most often during winter months, East Hawaiʻi Island, the entire island, or even the entire state can be affected. Most vog generated by Kīlauea stays below 6,000 to 8,000 feet above sea level, the usual height of the trade wind inversion, which is why the summits of Mauna Loa and Mauna Kea often sit above the vog layer.

  • Trade winds running: haze around the south of the island and along the Kona coast.
  • Trade winds absent: haze in East Hawaiʻi, island-wide, or statewide.
  • Above roughly 6,000 to 8,000 feet: usually above the vog layer.

USGS names the sensitive groups most likely to experience health impacts: people with asthma, lung or heart problems, older adults, infants and children, and pregnant women. The Hawaiʻi Department of Health adds outdoor workers and people exercising outdoors. Physically active asthmatics are most likely to experience serious effects from sulfur dioxide, and even short-term exposure can narrow the airways. If you have asthma, keep your medication available and use it as prescribed.

The short-term symptoms listed for vog exposure are eye, nose, throat, and skin irritation, coughing or phlegm, chest tightness or shortness of breath, headache, aggravation of asthma, fatigue or dizziness, and nausea. At sulfur dioxide levels considered unhealthy for the general population, even non-asthmatics may experience breathing difficulties.

sections.h2: Checking the air before you commit to a day
sections.body:
Sulfur dioxide and PM2.5 are measured inside Hawaiʻi Volcanoes National Park and across Hawaiʻi Island by the state Department of Health Clean Air Branch, the National Park Service, and the USGS Hawaiian Volcano Observatory, with a public network of low-cost PurpleAir sensors filling gaps. The Hawaiʻi Interagency Vog Information Dashboard collects those readings alongside vog forecast tools. It is a collaboration of the International Volcanic Health Hazard Network, the state Department of Health, USGS Hawaiian Volcano Observatory, Hawaiʻi County Civil Defense, the National Park Service, the County of Hawaiʻi, the Center for the Study of Active Volcanoes at the University of Hawaiʻi, NOAA's National Weather Service, and the USDA Farm Service Agency.

The practical version: check the dashboard or AirNow before you commit to a day, look at wind direction, and put the hard outdoor thing on a day the trades are running.

sections.h2: What helps, and what does not
sections.body:
Standard guidance for a high-vog day is to reduce outdoor activities, go indoors and close all doors and windows, seal gaps under doors and around windows, set air conditioners to recirculate, keep medications on hand and use them as prescribed, and drink plenty of liquids. An appropriate air-cleaning device reduces sulfur dioxide and PM2.5 in a sealed room or home.

What does not work is a mask. The Hawaiʻi Department of Health does not recommend the use of respirators by the general public to protect against volcanic gases. N95 masks can help protect against volcanic ash but not against gases such as sulfur dioxide, and most common masks and bandanas will not provide substantial protection from PM2.5 or sulfur dioxide. Facial hair prevents a tight seal, and N95s carry their own risks for children and people with respiratory conditions. The Department of Health does recommend N95 masks, heavy-duty gloves, long clothing, shoes, and eye protection for cleanup in ash-affected areas. If you drive near volcanic emissions, temporarily close your windows and turn the fan and air conditioner off.

sections.h2: Hawaiʻi Volcanoes National Park in particular
sections.body:
The eruption is occurring within a closed area of the park. The park runs an air quality alert page and advises checking air quality frequently during your visit, because hazardous volcanic gases can present a danger to sensitive groups. Rangers close areas when conditions warrant; follow ranger instructions and posted closures.

Lava fountains create tephra: small glassy volcanic fragments including volcanic ash, pumice, scoria, Pele's hair, and reticulite. Larger particles fall near the vents while light particles can be carried greater distances, and they can be remobilized during windy conditions after a recent episode. A light fall of Pele's hair was reported at several sites in the park outside the closed area after episode 51, including Uēkahuna overlook and the Kaʻū Desert trailhead on Highway 11. USGS advises minimizing exposure to these fragments, which can cause skin, eye, and respiratory irritation.

The park is partway through a two-year construction project at the summit to repair or remove damaged buildings and infrastructure, so expect closures and delays. Entrance is $30 per private vehicle, valid seven days, and the park does not accept cash. Parking lots can be full by 10 a.m.

Kīlauea has been erupting episodically at Halemaʻumaʻu since December 23, 2024, and fountaining episodes generally last less than 12 hours.
Pauses between fountaining episodes can be longer than three weeks.
Between episodes, summit sulfur dioxide output typically varies within a range of 1,000 to 5,000 tonnes per day.
From May through September the trade winds blow 80 to 95 percent of the time, carrying vog around the south of the island and along the Kona coast.
When trade winds are absent, most often in winter, East Hawaiʻi Island, the entire island, or the entire state can be affected.
Most Kīlauea vog stays below 6,000 to 8,000 feet, the usual height of the trade wind inversion.
The Hawaiʻi Department of Health does not recommend respirators for the general public against volcanic gases; N95s help against ash, not sulfur dioxide.

internalLinks.label: What to pack for the Big Island

cautions: If you have asthma or a chronic lung or heart condition, carry your medication daily and treat a high-vog day as a reason to change the plan, not push through it.

Do not rely on an N95 or dust mask for vog. N95s can help against volcanic ash but not against sulfur dioxide gas, and the state Department of Health does not recommend respirators for the general public against volcanic gases.

At sulfur dioxide levels considered unhealthy for the general population, even non-asthmatics may experience breathing difficulties. Follow ranger instructions and posted closures at Hawaiʻi Volcanoes National Park without exception.

Pele's hair and other glassy tephra can fall downwind after a fountaining episode and can be remobilized by wind afterward. These fragments cause skin, eye, and respiratory irritation; minimize exposure.

Air quality tells you nothing about the water. Surf, current, and shorebreak are independent of vog, and many Big Island beaches have no lifeguard. Check live beach conditions before you get in, every time.

title: What to Pack for the Big Island (Including the Cold Parts)
targetQuery: what to pack big island hawaii
intro: Conditions on Hawaiʻi Island run from hot and dry on the Kona coast to wet on the Hilo side, cool and rainy at Kīlauea's summit near 4,000 feet, and below freezing on Mauna Kea in any month. Packing for one climate is how people end up cold at 9,200 feet and soaked at the volcano on the same trip. Pack for all four, and expect to carry layers rather than leave them in the car.

sections.h2: The cold parts, which are real
sections.body:
Two places on this island get genuinely cold. Mauna Kea's summit is 13,803 feet and the Visitor Information Station sits at 9,200 feet. The mountain's safety guidance states that winter conditions may occur at any time, causing freezing temperatures, 100-plus mph winds, and zero-visibility whiteouts. Hypothermia is a listed hazard, with instructions to be prepared for winter weather, use adequate cold-weather clothing, and limit your exposure to the cold. A hoodie is not that. Read the Mauna Kea guide before you go up.

The second is Kīlauea's summit area in Hawaiʻi Volcanoes National Park, around 4,000 feet, where the Park Service says temperatures may be 12 to 15 degrees cooler than at sea level and it can be rainy and chilly any time of the year.

sections.h2: Rain gear for the east side and the park
sections.body:
The windward side, from Hilo through Hāmākua and down the Puna coast, is the wet side of the island, and passing showers are normal on otherwise sunny days. A light packable rain shell is worth the space. Quick-dry layers beat cotton once you are on a muddy trail.

The coastal end of the park, at the bottom of Chain of Craters Road, is the opposite. The Park Service describes it as often hot, dry, and windy with the possibility of passing showers. One park visit can go from cold rain at the caldera to open sun at the coast, so carry the layers with you instead of leaving them in the car at the trailhead.

The leeward Kona coast is dry and exposed. A wide-brim hat, sunglasses, and a rash guard or long-sleeve sun shirt cut down how much sunscreen you have to keep reapplying. Sunglasses matter at elevation too: intense solar radiation is a listed hazard on Mauna Kea, where the guidance is to protect yourself with appropriate clothing, sunscreen, and sunglasses.

Bring a refillable water bottle per person. The summit air on Mauna Kea is extremely dry, and the suggested intake there is about 16.9 fluid ounces (500 ml) per person per hour.

sections.h2: Sunscreen and what you can buy here
sections.body:
Hawaiʻi County Ordinance 22-81, from Bill 167, took effect December 1, 2022. It makes it unlawful to sell, offer for sale, or distribute for sale any non-mineral sunscreen in the county without a prescription issued by a licensed health care provider. Only titanium dioxide and zinc oxide are permitted as active ingredients. Unlike Maui County's ordinance, the Hawaiʻi County rule restricts sale rather than use, so a chemical sunscreen you brought from home is not prohibited.

Pack mineral sunscreen before you come. Do not plan on picking up your usual brand once you land, because it may not be on the shelf anywhere in the county.

Much of this island is rock. Beach entries at places like Hōnaunau Bay are lava ledge rather than sand, and park trails cross broken ʻaʻā and glassy pāhoehoe that will cut a bare foot and wear through a thin sole. Bring closed-toe shoes with real grip for trails, and water shoes or reef booties for rocky entries.

Rubber slippers are fine for town and for the sand at Hāpuna or Kua Bay. They are not fine on a lava trail or a wet rock ledge. Pack both, and accept that one pair of shoes will not cover this island.

Worth the space in the bag:

  • Respiratory and heart medication in your carry-on and then in your day bag. Vog is routine on the Kona side; see the vog guide.
  • A portable battery, since you will use the phone as a camera all day.
  • Offline maps downloaded in advance. Cell-phone service on Mauna Kea is spotty and absent in places, and above the Visitor Information Station phone use is restricted to emergencies.
  • A dry bag for phone and keys at rocky beaches with no place to set anything down.
  • Your own mask and snorkel if you own them. Rental gear that leaks is a safety problem, not an inconvenience.
  • A headlamp for pre-dawn drives and for walking back from a sunset spot.

Skip the bulky gear you can rent locally. Do not skip the warm layer, which is the one thing you cannot improvise at 9,200 feet at 9 p.m.

keyFacts: Mauna Kea's summit is 13,803 feet, and its safety guidance warns that winter conditions may occur at any time, causing freezing temperatures, 100-plus mph winds, and whiteouts.
The Maunakea Visitor Information Station is at 9,200 feet, where adequate cold-weather clothing is part of the official guidance.
Kīlauea's summit area sits near 4,000 feet, where temperatures may be 12 to 15 degrees cooler than at sea level, and it can be rainy and chilly any time of the year.
The coastal end of Chain of Craters Road is often hot, dry, and windy with possible passing showers, so one park visit can require both rain gear and sun gear.
Hawaiʻi County Ordinance 22-81 has made it unlawful to sell, offer for sale, or distribute for sale non-mineral sunscreen in the county since December 1, 2022.
Only titanium dioxide and zinc oxide are permitted as active ingredients in sunscreen sold in Hawaiʻi County.
The county sunscreen rule restricts sale and distribution rather than use, so sunscreen brought from home is not prohibited.
Hawaiʻi Volcanoes National Park entry is $30 per private vehicle for seven days, and the park does not accept cash.
cautions: Water shoes protect your feet on lava and reef. They do not make dangerous water safe. Check live conditions before entering, stay out when waves are breaking onto rock, and remember that many Big Island beaches have no lifeguard.

Underdressing for Mauna Kea is a health risk, not just discomfort. Hypothermia is a listed hazard at the Visitor Information Station and above, and freezing temperatures and 100-plus mph winds can occur in any month.
Keep asthma and heart medication on you during the day rather than at the hotel. Vog levels shift with wind direction through the day.
Do not walk lava trails in sandals. The rock is broken and sharp, and footwear with grip and a real sole is the only thing between you and it.

title: The Kona Manta Ray Night Snorkel: How It Works and How to Do It Safely
intro: Kona's manta ray night snorkel puts you in the ocean after dark to watch reef mantas feed. Boats leave around sunset from Keauhou Bay and from Honokōhau Harbor north of Kailua-Kona, stop over a lit patch of sand, and you float face-down holding a lighted board while the mantas eat the plankton the lights gather. It is open water, at night, off a boat, and it is not risk-free.

sections.body:
The lights are the whole mechanism. Downward-facing lights gather plankton, the mantas come to eat the plankton, and you watch from a few feet away. Snorkelers hang on a floating light board at the surface with their legs up and still. Scuba divers stay on the sand at the bottom. The water column in between is left empty so the animals have room to loop and barrel-roll through it.

Most of the trip is briefing, transit, and gear, and the time actually in the water is a much shorter window than the trip length suggests. Floating still at the surface after dark gets cold, so ask whether the boat provides wetsuits.

The state has designated two manta ray viewing zones in West Hawaiʻi, both inside the West Hawaiʻi Ocean Recreation Management Area: Makako Bay, known in daylight as Garden Eel Cove, offshore of the Kona airport, and Kaukalaelae Point at Keauhou Bay south of Kailua-Kona.

Which one you go to matters less than how long the boat ride is. If anyone in your group gets seasick, that difference is the whole evening. Check live conditions the afternoon of your trip, because Kona's leeward water is usually calmer than the windward side but not always calm.

Do not touch a manta. Their skin carries a protective mucus layer that a hand wipes off. Do not chase one, do not swim under one, and do not free-dive down to get a photo from below. Manta rays have no stinging barb, which is exactly why people forget themselves and reach out. Keep your hands to your chest.

This is also the law. Hawaiʻi Revised Statutes §188-39.5 makes it illegal to knowingly capture, take, possess, abuse, or entangle a ray, or to kill one, in state marine waters. Criminal fines run $500 for a first offense, $2,000 for a second, and $10,000 for a third or later offense, with administrative fines of up to $10,000 per ray on top of that.

sections.h2: The Green List, and what it means that it is gone
sections.body:
Hawaii Ocean Watch ran a Manta Ray Green List that certified operators against a written standard of conduct. It suspended the list in 2023, saying it had become virtually impossible for companies operating at the Keauhou or airport viewing sites to comply, with 15 to 30 boats dwelling or circulating in the dark while 200 to 400 people were in the water.

The standards themselves are still a usable yardstick, whether or not anyone is certifying against them:

  • No touching a manta.
  • No free diving down to the animals.
  • No lights mounted on the boat hull.
  • No propellers.
  • No anchoring on reef.
  • No fragmenting the group.

sections.h2: There are still no state rules
sections.body:
This is the part most booking pages leave out. There is no adopted state rule specific to manta viewing. In October 2022 the Board of Land and Natural Resources approved starting rulemaking for the two West Hawaiʻi zones. The proposal would limit commercial viewing permits to 24 in each zone, define manta ray viewing hours as 4:00 p.m. to 4:00 a.m. the next day, run vessels in two-hour shifts in each zone, allow no more than 60 passengers for hire per boat within any 24-hour period, require a guide-to-customer ratio of 8-to-1, and charge a fixed monthly fee of $300 on top of commercial use permit fees.

None of that is in force. No manta ray viewing rules appear among the adopted ocean recreation rules the Division of Boating and Ocean Recreation lists, which carry amendments dated through April 2025. Until rules are adopted, the number of boats on any given night, and the conduct on them, depends on the company you picked.

On April 30, 2025, a 62-year-old visitor from Portland, Oregon died after a guided manta ray snorkel out of Keauhou Pier. Police say she was in the water about five minutes, returned to the boat saying her arms were sore and that she was not feeling well, then became unresponsive shortly afterward. Crew members administered CPR and she was pronounced dead at Kona Community Hospital. Police opened a coroner's inquest to determine the cause of death and said no foul play was suspected.

Stack the conditions honestly. It is dark. You cannot stand up. You are in open water off a boat, sometimes among many boats. You are floating still and getting cold. If you are not a comfortable swimmer, if you have a heart or lung condition, or if you have never worn a snorkel before, this is the wrong trip for your first attempt. Try a mask in daylight somewhere shallow first, like Kahaluʻu Beach Park, and see how breathing through it feels.

Sightings are not guaranteed, and operators handle a no-show night differently, so ask what their policy actually is before you pay. Ask how many people are on the board, whether wetsuits are included, whether they run a separate float for weak swimmers, and how they handle someone who wants out early.

Book early in your trip so a weather cancellation leaves you a second shot. Go on a night you are rested, not the night you landed. If the crew cancels for conditions, that is the system working.

keyFacts: Hawaiʻi has two designated manta ray viewing zones in West Hawaiʻi: Makako Bay (Garden Eel Cove) off the Kona airport and Kaukalaelae Point at Keauhou Bay, both inside the West Hawaiʻi Ocean Recreation Management Area.
There is no adopted state rule specific to manta viewing; the Board of Land and Natural Resources approved starting rulemaking on October 27, 2022.

The proposed rules would limit commercial viewing permits to 24 per zone, set viewing hours of 4:00 p.m. to 4:00 a.m., run two-hour vessel shifts, cap boats at 60 passengers for hire per 24 hours, require an 8-to-1 guide-to-customer ratio, and charge $300 monthly.
Hawaiʻi Revised Statutes §188-39.5 makes it illegal to knowingly capture, take, possess, abuse, or entangle a ray, or to kill one, in state marine waters.
Criminal fines under §188-39.5 run $500 for a first offense, $2,000 for a second, and $10,000 for a third or later offense, with administrative fines up to $10,000 per ray.
Hawaii Ocean Watch suspended its Manta Ray Green List in 2023, citing 15 to 30 boats circulating in the dark while 200 to 400 people were in the water.
The Green List standards were: no touching, no free diving, no hull lighting, no propellers, no anchoring on reef, and no fragmentation of the group.
A 62-year-old visitor from Portland, Oregon died after a guided manta snorkel out of Keauhou Pier on April 30, 2025; police opened a coroner's inquest and suspect no foul play.
