Things to do on the Big Island

cautions: This is open water at night, off a boat, with no bottom under you. Calm-looking water is not safe water. Check live conditions, and if breathing through the snorkel feels like effort at any point, get back on the boat immediately.
Never touch, chase, or dive down on a manta. Handling a ray is a crime under Hawaiʻi law, with criminal fines up to $10,000 and administrative fines up to $10,000 per animal.
Do not make this your first time in a mask. Test your gear in shallow daylight water where you can stand before committing to a night trip in open water.

No state rules govern these tours yet, so crowding and conduct vary entirely by company. Ask how many boats and people are typically at the site on your night, and book the operator that answers straight.
Cold and seasickness end more of these trips than anything else. Ask whether wetsuits are included, and take motion-sickness medication before boarding, not after.

title: Whale Watching on the Big Island: Season, Where, and How
intro: Humpbacks come to Hawaiʻi in winter to breed and calve, then return to Alaska. NOAA's sanctuary gives the viewing window as November through April. Hawaiʻi's tourism authority lists December to May for Hawaiʻi Island. On the Big Island you do not need a boat. The Kohala Coast has enough elevated shoreline to watch from land for free, and Puʻukoholā Heiau above Kawaihae Harbor is the site the state names first.

sections.body:
The Hawaiian Islands Humpback Whale National Marine Sanctuary says that from November through April, visitors can see whales from shore and at sea. Go Hawaiʻi lists December to May for Hawaiʻi Island. The two windows overlap from December through April, which is the stretch to plan a trip around.

The sanctuary's Ocean Count gives a sense of scale. In 2025, 1,353 volunteers counted whales from 44 different sites across Hawaiʻi Island, Maui, Molokaʻi, Lānaʻi, Oʻahu, and Kauaʻi. A total of 4,782 humpbacks were counted over the event's three days.

Shore watching costs nothing and works well here. You want height and an open western horizon. Puʻukoholā Heiau National Historic Site above Kawaihae Harbor is the site Go Hawaiʻi calls out first, and the Kohala beaches give you long open water. Bring binoculars. Look for the puff of a spout first, then keep your eyes on that patch of water for several minutes rather than scanning.

Reasonable places to stand and look:

  • Puʻukoholā Heiau National Historic Site, on the bluff above Kawaihae.
  • Hāpuna Beach, for a wide open western view.
  • Kaunaʻoa Beach, at the north end of the same stretch.
  • Hilo Bay on the east side, which Go Hawaiʻi also names.

Wind generally builds through the day, so morning is usually the easiest time to read the water surface.

Two harbors serve most trips. Honokōhau Harbor sits about three miles north of Kailua-Kona, at the south end of Kaloko-Honokōhau National Historical Park, and is the closest launch to the Kona hotels. Kawaihae Harbor is the shorter drive from the Kohala Coast resorts. Both put you in leeward water on the west side of the island, which is the practical argument for doing this on the Kona side at all.

Because wind builds through the day, morning departures are generally smoother than afternoon ones. Small rafts sit lower to the water and take more of a beating; larger catamarans are steadier if anyone in the group is prone to seasickness. Take motion-sickness medication before you board.

Federal law prohibits approaching within 100 yards of a humpback whale in Hawaiʻi. That applies by boat, by kayak, by drone, when swimming, or by any other vessel or means. It is not a courtesy guideline, and it does not stop applying because the whale came to you.

If you are running a boat and end up within 100 yards, NOAA's instruction is to stop immediately, leave the engines running and out of gear, and wait until the whale moves away. NOAA also recommends a top speed of 15 knots or safe planing speed while transiting, and a maximum of six knots within 400 yards of a whale until you are more than 400 yards off. Report suspected violations to NOAA Fisheries Enforcement at (800) 853-1964.

Congress created the sanctuary in 1992 to protect humpbacks and their habitat. It lies in the shallow waters surrounding the main Hawaiian Islands, less than 600 feet deep, and is made up of five separate areas abutting six of the main islands. The Hawaiʻi Island piece is the sanctuary's southeastern-most section, about 150 square miles.

Worth being clear about: the 100-yard approach rule is federal law throughout Hawaiʻi, not something that switches on only when you cross a sanctuary line. Inside the boundary off Kawaihae or well outside it, the distance is the same.

sections.h2: The other animals you will see
sections.body:
Spinner dolphins are common in the same leeward bays and carry their own federal limit: it is illegal to swim with, approach, or remain within 50 yards of a spinner dolphin in Hawaiʻi. They rest in shallow water during the day, and a boat or swimmer pushing in on a resting pod is doing real harm even when the dolphins look playful.

Green sea turtles are common along this coast. NOAA gives at least 10 feet, on land and in the water, as the recommended viewing distance for them, at least 50 feet for Hawaiian monk seals, and at least 150 feet for a mother seal with a pup. Those are recommended distances; the 100-yard humpback limit and the 50-yard spinner dolphin limit are federal law. Go Hawaiʻi also notes other whale species are in these waters year round, so a sighting outside the humpback window is not impossible. Check live conditions before any shoreline outing, and see the manta ray night snorkel guide for the island's other well-known wildlife trip.

keyFacts: NOAA's sanctuary gives the humpback viewing window as November through April; Go Hawaiʻi lists December to May for Hawaiʻi Island.
In the 2025 Sanctuary Ocean Count, 1,353 volunteers counted 4,782 humpback whales from 44 sites across six islands over the event's three days.
Federal law prohibits approaching within 100 yards of a humpback whale in Hawaiʻi, including by boat, kayak, drone, or while swimming.
A boat within 100 yards of a humpback must stop immediately and leave engines running and out of gear until the whale moves away.
NOAA recommends a 15-knot top speed while transiting and a maximum of six knots within 400 yards of a whale.
Suspected violations are reported to NOAA Fisheries Enforcement at (800) 853-1964.
Congress created the sanctuary in 1992; it lies in water less than 600 feet deep across five separate areas abutting six main islands, with about 150 square miles along Hawaiʻi Island.

Federal law prohibits swimming with, approaching, or remaining within 50 yards of spinner dolphins; NOAA recommends at least 10 feet from sea turtles and 50 feet from monk seals, or 150 feet for a mother with a pup.
cautions: Whale season is also winter surf season. Shore watching pulls people onto rocks, bluffs, and wave-exposed points for a better angle. Check live conditions, keep back from the wet zone on any lava shelf, and never turn your back on the water.
Stay 100 yards from humpbacks by any means, including swimming and drones. If a whale surfaces near you, stop and let it move off rather than closing the gap.
Do not approach or swim with spinner dolphins. Federal law sets a 50-yard limit, and the shallow bays they use during the day are where they rest.
Open-channel boat trips get rougher as the wind builds through the day. Take motion-sickness medication before boarding, and pick a morning departure if anyone in the group is prone to it.
Use binoculars from a fixed vantage point rather than walking out onto wet rock for a closer angle. Surf breaking over a low shelf is the hazard on this coast, not the whales.

title: Where to See Sea Turtles on the Big Island (Respectfully)
targetQuery: big island sea turtles where to see
intro: Green sea turtles are common in shallow water around Hawaiʻi Island, and the green is the only sea turtle here that hauls out on sand to rest. This guide covers three areas: Punaluʻu in Kaʻū, Kahaluʻu in Kona, and the shallow lava coves on the Hilo side. NOAA Fisheries and Hawaiʻi DLNR both put the viewing distance at ten feet, on land and in the water. Here is where to look and how to behave.

sections.h2: Two species, and you will see the common one
sections.body:
The turtle you will meet is the green sea turtle, honu. DLNR calls it the most frequently observed sea turtle swimming in Hawaiian waters and the only sea turtle in Hawaiʻi that basks on the beach. Green sea turtles can weigh over 350 pounds, measure three to four feet in length, and are estimated to live 70 years or more. Hawaiʻi's greens are classified within the Central North Pacific distinct population segment, which NOAA Fisheries lists as threatened under the Endangered Species Act.

The other one is the hawksbill, honuʻea, named for its beak. It is far rarer. DLNR says greens outnumber hawksbills in Hawaiʻi by about 100 to one, and hawksbills are listed as endangered throughout their global range. Hawksbills do not bask, and adults are not typically seen on land unless a female is crawling up the beach at night to dig a nest, or the animal is injured, sick, or dead.

All sea turtles in Hawaiʻi are protected by the federal Endangered Species Act and by Hawaiʻi Revised Statutes Chapter 195D and Hawaiʻi Administrative Rules 13-124. You do not need to identify the species to know the rules apply.

Punaluʻu sits on the southeast coast between Pāhala and Nāʻālehu, in the Kaʻū district. The Hawaiʻi Tourism Authority's visitor site says you may find large honu basking on the beach here, and there is a picnic area and restroom facilities. Its guidance is direct about two things: do not touch these protected turtles, and do not remove any black sand from the beach. The same page says swimming here is not ideal.

Treat it as a viewing beach. OceanSafe flags Punaluʻu as a hazard-warning beach with only seasonal lifeguard coverage, and the activities it is listed for are walking, tidepools, and photography, not swimming or snorkeling. A turtle sitting comfortably in the shallows tells you nothing about whether the water is safe for you. Check live conditions at Punaluʻu before you go anywhere near the water line.

Kahaluʻu is a shallow bay on Aliʻi Drive south of Kailua-Kona, and the Kohala Center describes it as part of the longest, interconnected coral reef in the main Hawaiian Islands. Adult honu are primarily herbivorous and feed mostly on limu, the macroalgae growing on shallow reef, so people regularly see them from the surface with a mask on. Nearly half a million people visit Kahaluʻu each year.

The park is open 7 a.m. to 7 p.m. daily. Lifeguards are on duty 9:30 a.m. to 4:30 p.m., and the Kohala Center strongly recommends waiting until the lifeguards are on duty before entering the water. ReefTeach volunteers staff the beach 8:30 a.m. to 3 p.m. and the site asks you to check in with one before you get in. Nonresident parking is $12 for four hours; Hawaiʻi residents with valid ID always park free. Visitors are asked to use mineral sunscreen only, meaning zinc oxide and/or titanium dioxide as the only active ingredients, and free dispensers run 9 a.m. to 3 p.m. daily.

Use the channel in front of the lifeguard tower, to the left of the pavilion, to enter and exit the bay. Avoid walking across the rocks. The Kohala Center says they are slippery, sharp, and an important feeding area for fish and honu. Give every turtle 10 feet. See today's conditions at Kahaluʻu.

sections.h2: The Hilo side: Richardson and Carlsmith
sections.body:
Green sea turtle feeding grounds are commonly associated with coral reefs and shallow areas such as rocky outcroppings and algal beds, which is what the small lava-rock coves of East Hawaiʻi are. Richardson Ocean Park and Carlsmith Beach Park are the two most useful stops. Both have full-time lifeguards in our data, and both are flagged as suitable for kids.

These coves are small, so a turtle grazing in one can put you closer to it than you intended. If that happens, stop swimming, stay still, and let it move. Do not follow it around the cove. Visibility drops after heavy rain, which the Hilo side gets a lot of.

sections.h2: Ten feet, on land and in the water
sections.body:
NOAA Fisheries gives the same number DLNR does for sea turtles: at least 10 feet, about 3 meters, away, on land and in the water. DLNR describes this as the current federal guideline for safe public viewing. It is a different number from the ones for other species you might run into here. Hawaiian monk seals require at least 50 feet, and 150 feet if a mother has a pup. Spinner dolphins require 50 yards, and federal law prohibits swimming with, approaching, or remaining within that distance. Humpback whales require 100 yards, also prohibited by federal regulation.

NOAA's instruction is to never touch, chase, or feed, and not to disturb sea turtles sleeping on the beach. DLNR adds that even non-life-threatening contact such as touching, feeding, or getting too close can cause stress and overexertion, and that turtles have powerful beaks and can seriously injure you with a bite. A honu asleep on the sand is doing a normal thing and does not need help. Keep dogs leashed and away from basking sea turtles and from known nesting beaches.

DLNR's position on enforcement is short: because the Endangered Species Act and state laws protect all sea turtles, violations of harassment or intentionally harming a turtle can result in significant fines or even time in jail. If you see someone or a pet disturbing or illegally interacting with a sea turtle, call NOAA's Office of Law Enforcement at (800) 853-1964 or DLNR's DOCARE at (808) 643-DLNR, or send photos and video to respectwildlife@noaa.gov.

sections.h2: Hawksbills, and why the Kaʻū coast matters
sections.body:
Hawksbill nesting in Hawaiʻi appears to be exclusive to the main Hawaiian Islands, and DLNR says it happens primarily along the southeast shoreline of the island of Hawaiʻi, on the remote Kaʻū coastline. The estimated average is only 20 to 25 females nesting annually, typically from May to December, with an average clutch of about 130 to 160 eggs and hatchlings generally emerging after about two months of incubation.

Green turtles nest on a different calendar, late April through late October, and DLNR estimates 96 percent of Hawaiʻi's green sea turtle population nests at French Frigate Shoals, a small atoll in the Northwestern Hawaiian Islands rather than anywhere you can drive to.

Practically, this means the empty-looking Kaʻū beaches are the sensitive ones. Hawksbill eggs and hatchlings are threatened by non-native cats, dogs, mongooses, rats, and pigs, and by non-native vegetation whose dense roots can block nest excavation or trap hatchlings. Light pollution and coastal development can prevent or delay hatchlings from finding the water. DLNR's guidance is to use shielded yellow or amber lighting near the coast, keep lights and beach fires to a minimum during nesting season, roughly April through December, and avoid beach driving in nesting areas.

Keep the distance rather than closing it. In the water, hold still and let the animal decide how close it wants to be, and back off if it changes direction. DLNR's summary of the whole thing is that the best thing to do is give them space.

Do not touch any turtle, including one with visible tumors. Fibropapillomatosis is caused by a herpes virus transmitted between turtles, and its tumors can exist externally and internally anywhere on the body, impairing sight, swimming, feeding, and buoyancy, or disrupting organ function. No methods currently exist for controlling or treating it.

Fishing line, hooks, and nets pose the greatest entanglement risk, because they can wrap around a turtle's limbs and stop it surfacing to breathe. Pick up any line or debris you find on the shoreline. Report a hooked, entangled, or injured turtle, and any hawksbill sighting, to 1-888-256-9840. Marine debris can be reported to 833-432-6387.

The reef the turtles are eating is the same reef the sunscreen rules exist for. Use mineral sunscreen with zinc oxide or titanium dioxide, or cover up with a shirt. Then read the snorkel safety guide, because the reefs where turtles feed are also where visitors get into trouble.

keyFacts: Hawaiʻi's green sea turtles belong to the Central North Pacific DPS, listed as threatened under the Endangered Species Act, and all sea turtles here are additionally protected by HRS Chapter 195D and HAR 13-124.
NOAA Fisheries and Hawaiʻi DLNR both give a viewing distance of at least 10 feet (3 meters) from a sea turtle, on land and in the water.
The green sea turtle is the only sea turtle in Hawaiʻi that basks on the beach, so a honu resting on the sand is behaving normally.
DLNR says green sea turtles outnumber hawksbills in Hawaiʻi by about 100 to one, and hawksbills are listed as endangered throughout their global range.
Hawksbills nest primarily along the remote Kaʻū coastline of Hawaiʻi Island, with an estimated average of only 20 to 25 females nesting annually, typically May to December.
Kahaluʻu Beach Park is open 7 a.m. to 7 p.m., lifeguards are on duty 9:30 a.m. to 4:30 p.m., and nonresident parking is $12 for four hours while Hawaiʻi residents with valid ID park free.
Kahaluʻu asks visitors to use mineral sunscreen only, with zinc oxide and/or titanium dioxide as the sole active ingredients, and free dispensers run 9 a.m. to 3 p.m. daily.
Illegal disturbance of a sea turtle can be reported to NOAA Office of Law Enforcement at (800) 853-1964 or DLNR DOCARE at (808) 643-DLNR, with photos to respectwildlife@noaa.gov.

cautions: Punaluʻu is a viewing beach. It carries a hazard warning in our data, is guarded only seasonally, and the Hawaiʻi Tourism Authority's own page says swimming there is not ideal. A turtle resting in the shallows tells you nothing about whether the water is safe for you.

Stay 10 feet back on land and in the water, and never touch, chase, or feed a honu. DLNR says violations of harassment or intentionally harming a turtle can result in significant fines or even time in jail.
Do not touch a turtle even when it looks approachable. DLNR warns they have powerful beaks and can seriously injure you with a bite, and that touching or crowding causes stress and overexertion.
Do not walk across the rocks at Kahaluʻu. The Kohala Center says they are slippery, sharp, and an important feeding area for fish and honu, and that sea urchins are among the common hazards.

Conditions at Kahaluʻu can change rapidly, and large waves, strong currents, sharp rocks, and sea urchins are common. The Kohala Center strongly recommends waiting until lifeguards are on duty at 9:30 a.m. before entering the water.

title: Snorkel Safety on the Big Island: Where People Get in Trouble
intro: Snorkeling causes more ocean drowning deaths among visitors in Hawaiʻi than any other activity, and the study the state tourism authority funded concluded that the snorkel itself is part of the problem. Many of these deaths happen in calm water, often shortly after the person enters, and usually with no visible sign of distress. Here is what the state's own numbers say, and where on Hawaiʻi Island people run into trouble.

sections.h2: What the state's numbers actually show
sections.body:
Between 2014 and 2023, snorkeling accounted for 225 ocean drowning deaths in Hawaiʻi, more than any other activity. Swimming came in at 188. Of those 225 snorkeling deaths, 205 were visitors. Over the 2019 to 2023 window the Department of Health puts the visitor share of snorkeling victims at 91 percent, while visitors comprise about 12 percent of the state's de facto population.

Visitors have eight times the drowning fatality rate of residents. Drowning is the leading cause of fatal injuries among visitors in Hawaiʻi; among residents it is the fifth leading cause.

For this island specifically: Hawaiʻi Island recorded 114 fatal ocean drownings between 2013 and 2022, an average of 11 a year, with 54 percent of the victims visitors. Over 2019 to 2023, Hawaiʻi County's ocean drowning rate was 24.3 per 100,000, lower than Kauaʻi (49.1) and Maui (45.7) but above Honolulu County (17.7).

sections.h2: It is often not the water. It is the snorkel.
sections.body:
The Hawaiʻi Department of Health formed a Snorkel Safety Sub-Committee in October 2017 in response to frequent snorkel-related drownings, particularly among non-residents. Many of the incidents were puzzling: they often occurred in calm water, sometimes shortly after the person entered, and typically without any visible signs of distress. In January 2019 the Hawaiʻi Tourism Authority funded the resulting Snorkel Safety Study, led by Ralph Goto, pulmonologist Philip R. Foti, M.D., and Carol Wilcox.

Taken together, the study's findings showed that the problem is the snorkel. Breathing through a narrow tube creates resistance during inhalation, which lowers lung pressure and draws fluid from surrounding capillaries into the air spaces. Each subsequent inhalation draws in more, progressively cutting oxygen intake into the blood, and the snorkeler becomes short of breath. That oxygen shortage, hypoxia, leads to loss of muscle strength and confusion, then loss of consciousness and clinical death, sometimes within minutes of the first signs. The study named it Snorkel-Induced Rapid-Onset Pulmonary Edema, or SIROPE, and identifies it as a relative of the pulmonary edema already documented in scuba divers, long-distance swimmers, and mountain climbers.

The practical difference from a classic aspiration drowning is the apparent absence of a struggle. The study's own headline is worth repeating: snorkeling itself is a hazard, and recreational snorkeling is not a benign, low-risk activity, for experienced and inexperienced swimmers alike.

sections.h2: What to do the moment breathing gets hard
sections.body:
If you unexpectedly become short of breath, do not push on and do not try to power back to shore with the snorkel still in your mouth. The study is explicit that exertion while trying to reach shore or escape a current while continuing to breathe through a snorkel worsens the situation.

Remove your mask and snorkel. Get on your back. Signal for help. Then get to shore or to a boat the best way possible. Loss of strength and confusion are part of the same hypoxia sequence, and none of it is a reason to finish the swim first.

sections.h2: Your gear and your flight both matter
sections.body:
Dr. Foti built the Snorkel Airway Resistance Analyzer to measure inhalation resistance, and tested 49 snorkels: 16 simple ones, 29 with wet/dry mechanisms, and four full-face masks, each at three airflow levels. Resistance varied widely. Simpler snorkels generally had lower resistance, but because a tube can narrow internally, a visual assessment of the narrowest opening does not tell you which snorkels have the least resistance.

Full-face masks offered no inherent advantage or disadvantage on inhalation resistance. Their problems are mechanical: difficulty in urgent removal, inability to spit out the mouthpiece, trouble clearing water with a sharp breath, and they are unsafe for diving beneath the surface. Valve malfunction can lead to serious aspiration risk. The theory that carbon dioxide accumulating in the mask knocks snorkelers unconscious was examined and found not to be a physiologically viable explanation.

Then there is the flight. On long-distance flights the cabin is pressurized to simulate conditions between 8,500 and 9,500 feet, and passengers to Hawaiʻi often experience that for five to nine hours or more. Extended time in that environment can weaken lung walls and cause edema, often noticeable as swollen ankles, and it is more common in older individuals and those with heart issues. Lungs usually recover after a few days at sea level, which is why the study recommends considering a 2 to 3 day wait after extended air travel before snorkeling.

sections.h2: Heart health is the risk factor nobody checks
sections.body:
Dr. Foti examined Coroner's Office records from 2018 and 2019 to see whether autopsies could differentiate drowning by aspiration from drowning by SIROPE. They could not: both involved liquid-filled lungs and death by hypoxia. What the autopsies did reveal was pre-existing health conditions and a correlation between drownings and cardiac disease, especially elevated Left Ventricular End-Diastolic Pressure in older individuals. Drugs and alcohol were rarely factors.

The separate case studies investigation, in which Dr. Foti interviewed survey participants and reviewed their medical records, identified elevated LVEDP as a risk factor for SIROPE. The study's safety tip for anyone with a heart condition is one line: consider not snorkeling.

sections.h2: Where on this island people get in trouble
sections.body:
Kahaluʻu Beach Park takes nearly half a million visitors a year. It has lifeguards, but only from 9:30 a.m. to 4:30 p.m., and the Kohala Center strongly recommends waiting until they are on duty before entering the water. Conditions in the bay can change rapidly, and large waves, strong currents, sharp rocks, sea urchins, and other hazards are common. Use the channel in front of the lifeguard tower to enter and exit rather than picking your way over the rocks.

Hōnaunau Bay, the Two Step, has no lifeguard in our data. The entry is a lava shelf that the Park Service describes as uneven, loose, and sometimes wet and slippery, and the area is primarily a boat ramp, so you are sharing it with boat traffic. The Park Service warning for this coast is to never turn your back on the ocean, because large waves can appear with little or no warning. Check for high surf and high wind warnings before you leave.

The state's 2025 Hawaiʻi Water Safety Plan maps Hawaiʻi Island's drowning black spots by name. Several are places visitors go for the snorkeling or the photo:

  • Kealakekua Bay
  • 69 Beach (Waialea Bay)
  • Mahaiʻula
  • Hoʻokena Beach Park
  • Kehena Beach
  • Green Sands Beach (Papakōlea) and the South Point Lookout
  • Pololū Valley and Waipiʻo Valley
  • End of the Road, Aliʻi Drive in Kona

Lifeguards do not make a beach safe either. Hāpuna is guarded and State Parks still posts a warning about dangerous rip currents and pounding shore breaks during periods of high surf, with the plain instruction that waves over 3 feet high are for experts and all others should stay out of the water and away from the shoreline.

sections.h2: The rules that actually lower your odds
sections.body:
Ocean Safety on Hawaiʻi Island is administered by the Hawaiʻi Fire Department, with two Ocean Safety Captains overseeing Hilo and Kona. The 2025 state plan is candid that a small tax base funds ocean safety patrols for a large area of mostly remote coastlines, saturated by the same visitor loads as other counties. Of the 28 Hawaiʻi Island beaches OceanSafe tracks, 11 have lifeguards: nine year-round and two seasonal. Most of the coast has none.

The Snorkel Safety Study's own ten safety tips:

  • Swim at a lifeguarded beach.
  • If you can't swim, don't snorkel.
  • Familiarize yourself with your equipment in shallow water.
  • Swim with a buddy and keep an eye on your buddy.
  • Stay where you can touch the bottom and be confident before moving to deeper water.
  • If you have a heart condition, consider not snorkeling.
  • Check your location frequently, every 30 seconds.
  • If you unexpectedly become short of breath, remove your mask, get on your back, signal for help, and get out.
  • Do not exercise or increase exertion while breathing through a snorkel.
  • Consider waiting 2 to 3 days after extended air travel before snorkeling.

Check live conditions for the specific beach on the specific morning, and if you are going out mainly to see honu, read the sea turtle guide first so you know the distance rule before you are in the water with one.

Hawaiʻi Department of Health data for 2019–2023 puts the visitor share of snorkeling drowning victims at 91 percent, while visitors comprise about 12 percent of the state's de facto population.
Hawaiʻi Island recorded 114 fatal ocean drownings from 2013 to 2022, an average of 11 per year, and 54 percent of the victims were visitors.

The Snorkel Safety Study concluded that Snorkel-Induced Rapid-Onset Pulmonary Edema (SIROPE) is a common factor in many, if not most, snorkel-related drownings, and that it presents with few if any signs of distress.

The study tested 49 snorkels including four full-face masks at three airflow levels, and found that a visual assessment of the narrowest opening does not identify which snorkels have the least resistance.

The study recommends considering a 2 to 3 day wait after extended air travel before snorkeling, because cabins pressurized to an 8,500–9,500 foot equivalent for five to nine hours can weaken lung walls and cause edema.
Hawaiʻi's 2025 Water Safety Plan maps Kealakekua Bay, 69 Beach, Mahaiʻula, Hoʻokena, Kehena, Green Sands, the South Point Lookout, Pololū and Waipiʻo among Hawaiʻi Island's drowning black spots.
Of the 28 Hawaiʻi Island beaches OceanSafe tracks, 11 have lifeguards; Hōnaunau Bay (Two Step) is not one of them.
cautions: Calm water is not safe water. The Department of Health formed its snorkel subcommittee precisely because these drownings often occurred in calm water, sometimes shortly after entry, and typically without visible signs of distress.

If you unexpectedly become short of breath, remove your mask, get on your back, signal for help, and get out. The study is explicit that exertion while still breathing through the snorkel worsens the situation.

Hōnaunau Bay (Two Step) has no lifeguard in our data, an uneven, loose and slippery lava-shelf entry, and active boat traffic. The Park Service warns never to turn your back on the ocean here because large waves can appear with little or no warning.

Hāpuna has lifeguards and State Parks still warns of dangerous rip currents and pounding shore breaks during high surf, instructing that waves over 3 feet are for experts and all others should stay out of the water and away from the shoreline.

If you have a heart condition, the Snorkel Safety Study's advice is to consider not snorkeling. Elevated Left Ventricular End-Diastolic Pressure turned up repeatedly in the records, and an autopsy cannot distinguish SIROPE from aspiration drowning.

title: Big Island Driving Times: Between Towns, and Around the Island
intro: The Big Island covers 4,028 square miles, 63 percent of the Hawaiian archipelago's land area, and it drives like it. Two airports sit on opposite coasts about two hours apart. There is one fast road across the middle and one long road around the outside, and neither is quick. These are realistic drive times between the places you will actually go, plus the roads that cost more time than the map suggests.

sections.h2: Two airports, and they are not close
sections.body:
Kona International (KOA) is on the dry west side. Hilo International (ITO) is on the wet east side. The drive between them takes about 1.5 to 2 hours over Saddle Road. That single fact decides more of your trip than anything else you book. If your lodging is on the Kohala coast and your flight lands in Hilo, you have added roughly two hours to your arrival day and another two to your departure.

Flying into one airport and out of the other works well if you are crossing the island anyway. Before you book that way, check with your rental company whether it allows a one-way drop-off between KOA and ITO and what it charges, rather than assuming it is free.

sections.h2: Saddle Road, and the rental-car myth
sections.body:
Saddle Road is Route 200, renamed the Daniel K. Inouye Highway in 2013. It runs 52.7 miles across the middle of the island, passing between Mauna Kea and Mauna Loa, and reaches a maximum elevation of 6,632 feet in the Humuʻula Saddle. Most people still picture the old road: one narrow lane each way, blind rises, no shoulder. That road is gone. Sections were rebuilt and opened in 2007, 2009 and 2013, and Wikipedia's route description records that the entire road is now well paved, with a separate lane for trucks and slower cars on the uphill sections.

Rental companies used to prohibit their cars on Saddle Road. Most now allow it. Read your own agreement anyway, and note that two roads on this island are genuinely restricted no matter what your contract says: Waipiʻo Valley Road is closed to visitors, and the Mauna Kea summit road above the Visitor Information Station is unpaved and requires four-wheel drive in low range.

What has not changed is the crossing itself. It runs high and often through cloud, there is no fuel and nothing open along it, and phone coverage is patchy. Fill up in Waimea, Hilo or Kona first, and download your maps before you leave town.

Kailua-Kona town is a short drive from the airport, on the order of ten to fifteen minutes. Hāpuna and the Kohala resorts are north of the airport, well under an hour. Waimea is roughly an hour inland. Hilo is 1.5 to 2 hours over Saddle Road.

Hawaiʻi Volcanoes National Park is the long one, and here the Park Service publishes the numbers itself: 95 miles southeast from Kailua-Kona on Highway 11, a 2 to 2.5 hour drive, or 125 miles through Waimea and Hilo via Highways 19 and 11, which takes 2.5 to 3 hours. From Waikoloa it is 90 miles southeast on Highway 200, about 2 hours.

Hilo is the closest base to the volcano by a wide margin. The Park Service gives it as 30 miles southwest on Highway 11, a 45 minute drive. Waimea is roughly an hour up Highway 19, and the Waipiʻo Valley lookout is beyond it at the end of the Hāmākua coast.

Hilo also puts you nearest ʻAkaka Falls, the Puna coast and the Hāmākua waterfalls. It is a working town rather than a resort strip, and it rains: Hilo International Airport averaged about 127 inches of rain a year between 1981 and 2010, against about 19 inches at Kailua-Kona over the same period.

The ring is Highway 11 along the south and Highway 19 along the north. People try to drive it in one day. You can, but it is a long day behind the wheel and you see the island through a windshield. For scale, the Park Service puts Kailua-Kona to the volcano at 2 to 2.5 hours going south on Highway 11, and 2.5 to 3 hours going the other way through Waimea and Hilo, and that is before you stop anywhere.

Split it instead. South half one day: Kona, Kaʻū, Hawaiʻi Volcanoes, overnight in Volcano or Hilo. North half the next: Hilo, the Hāmākua coast, Waimea, Kohala. Same ground, and you actually get out of the car.

sections.h2: The roads that cost more time than the map says
sections.body:
Mauna Kea Access Road turns off Saddle Road near its high point. It is paved as far as the Visitor Information Station at 9,200 feet and unpaved above that. The University of Hawaiʻi at Hilo, which runs the station, states that drivers are required to use four-wheel drive above the VIS because the summit road is unpaved, rough and steep, that four-wheel-drive low range should always be used to reduce brake failure and overheating, and that you should have at least half a tank of fuel before going up. It also asks that vehicles be free of invasive species and that no muddy vehicles go to the summit. Plan to acclimatise at least 30 minutes at the station before climbing higher.

Waipiʻo Valley Road drops into the valley on a 25 percent average grade, with sections up to 45 percent, and is described as the steepest road of its length in the United States. Access to the valley floor by road is currently allowed only for island residents, county-permitted tour company operators, and people practising Native Hawaiian traditional or customary rights. The lookout at the top is open to everyone. Confirm the county's rule before you plan a day around it.

Kekaha Kai State Park is reached by a rough lava road off Highway 19 and is slow in any vehicle; the gates run 8:00 a.m. to 6:30 p.m. and close at 7:00 p.m. Chain of Craters Road inside Hawaiʻi Volcanoes leads down to the coast and dead-ends there, so everything you drive down you drive back up.

sections.h2: Small things that save an hour
sections.body:
Fuel up before Saddle Road, before the Kaʻū stretch and before the Puna coast. These are the three places on the island where the gap between stations is long enough to matter, and Naʻalehu is the practical stop in Kaʻū.

Do not book a sunset dinner on the day you drive to the volcano. Hawaiʻi Volcanoes is open 24 hours, viewing runs late, and the return to Kona is over two hours in the dark. The Park Service also warns that park parking lots frequently reach capacity by 10 a.m., so an early start or a late one beats mid-morning. Download offline maps before you go, because coverage is unreliable across Saddle Road, the summit road, Chain of Craters Road and the remoter parts of the Hāmākua and Puna coasts.

Saddle Road, Route 200, renamed the Daniel K. Inouye Highway in 2013, is 52.7 miles long and reaches a maximum elevation of 6,632 feet.
Rental companies used to prohibit Saddle Road and now generally allow it; the road was rebuilt in sections opened in 2007, 2009 and 2013.
The Park Service puts Hawaiʻi Volcanoes National Park at 30 miles and 45 minutes from Hilo, versus 95 miles and 2 to 2.5 hours from Kailua-Kona on Highway 11.
The alternative Kailua-Kona route to the park, through Waimea and Hilo on Highways 19 and 11, is 125 miles and 2.5 to 3 hours.

Waipiʻo Valley Road has a 25 percent average grade with sections up to 45 percent, and valley-floor access is limited to residents, county-permitted operators and Native Hawaiian traditional and customary practice.
Mauna Kea Access Road is paved only to the Visitor Information Station at 9,200 feet; above that, four-wheel drive in low range is required.
Hilo International Airport averaged about 127 inches of rain a year from 1981 to 2010; Kailua-Kona averaged about 19.

cautions: Saddle Road crosses high country that is frequently in cloud. Slow down in fog, use low beams, and do not pass on the climbs.

The Mauna Kea summit road above the Visitor Information Station is unpaved, rough and steep. Four-wheel drive in low range is required, there is no fuel on the mountain, and the station advises that children under 13, pregnant women, people who are intoxicated, people with high blood pressure or a heart or respiratory condition, and anyone who has scuba dived in the prior 24 hours should not go above it.

Nothing about a short drive makes the water safe. Only ten beaches on this island have lifeguards, on duty 9:30 a.m. to 4:45 p.m. daily. Check live conditions before you get in and choose a lifeguarded beach when you can.

title: First Time on the Big Island: What to Know Before You Land
targetQuery: first time big island what to know
intro: The Big Island is not a scaled-up Maui. It is 4,028 square miles with two airports on opposite coasts, a rainforest on one side and near-desert on the other, an erupting volcano in the middle, and ten lifeguarded beaches for the entire island. Most first-trip problems here are planning problems, not bad luck. Here is what to sort out before the plane doors open.

sections.h2: Pick the right airport, or use both
sections.body:
Kona International (KOA) serves the dry west side, the Kohala resorts and the coffee belt. Hilo International (ITO) serves the wet east side, the Hāmākua coast and Hawaiʻi Volcanoes National Park. They are about 1.5 to 2 hours apart over Saddle Road. Booking the wrong one can cost you four hours of driving on a short trip.

If your plan crosses the island anyway, flying into one and out of the other is usually the better trip. Rental companies charge a fee for a one-way drop-off between the two, so confirm it before you commit. The numbers are in the driving times guide.

The county Hele-On bus does reach Hawaiʻi Volcanoes National Park, dropping off and picking up at the intersection of Volcano House and the second entrance to Kīlauea Visitor Center, but the Park Service notes its schedules are subject to change and delays and that there is no public transport or shuttle within the park. It also states that the park sits 30 miles from the closest population centre with rideshare drivers, which makes rideshare apps very difficult and sometimes impossible to use there. Book the car when you book the flight.

Read the rental agreement's road exclusions. Saddle Road is usually fine now. Waipiʻo Valley Road is closed to visitors regardless, and the Mauna Kea summit road above the Visitor Information Station is unpaved and requires four-wheel drive in low range, so a tow off it is on you.

Hilo International Airport averaged about 127 inches of rain a year between 1981 and 2010. Kailua-Kona averaged about 19 over the same period, sheltered on the leeward side of Hualālai. A single forecast for the Big Island is nearly meaningless, because it is describing two different climates at once, plus a 13,803-foot mountain that gets snow.

Practically: pack a rain shell for the east side and a warm layer for the high country even in July, and do not cancel a Hilo day because the app says rain. Check the conditions where you actually are on the live conditions hub.

sections.h2: The volcano is erupting, on its own schedule
sections.body:
Kīlauea has been erupting episodically from Halemaʻumaʻu at the summit since December 23, 2024, and was still going through mid-2026, past its fiftieth episode. The Park Service puts the pattern plainly: eruptions can be as short as a few hours, and pauses between them last several days or weeks. Do not build a trip around seeing lava. Build it around seeing the park, and treat an active episode as a bonus.

Entry is $30 per private vehicle, valid seven days. The park does not accept cash, only credit or debit. The Hawaiʻi Tri-Park annual pass is $55 and also covers Haleakalā and Puʻuhonua o Hōnaunau. The park is open 24 hours a day, seven days a week, including holidays, which matters because the glow reads best after dark. The eruption area itself is closed; you view from open points along the caldera rim. The Park Service also warns of closures and delays from a two-year construction project repairing or removing damaged buildings and infrastructure at the summit, and that parking lots frequently fill by 10 a.m.

sections.h2: The ocean here is less forgiving than it looks
sections.body:
The state Department of Health counts an average of nearly 40 resident drowning deaths a year, rising to 83 when non-residents are included. Non-residents were the majority of victims at 53 percent over the 2013 to 2017 period, and the fatal ocean drowning rate for non-residents in Hawaiʻi is about eight times higher than for residents. The Big Island's non-resident fatal ocean drowning rate is 51.8 per 100,000, third among the main islands behind Kauaʻi at 82.5 and Maui at 64.6. The department also states that more Hawaiʻi visitors drown while snorkelling than during any other activity.

Ten beaches on this island have county lifeguards, on duty 9:30 a.m. to 4:45 p.m. daily. Everywhere else you are on your own, including some of the most photographed spots. The state's own park pages carry blunt warnings: Hāpuna and Kekaha Kai both warn of dangerous rip currents and pounding shore breaks during periods of high surf, and Kekaha Kai has no lifeguard services at all. Read the beaches guide before you pick a spot.

Vog forms when sulfur dioxide and other gases and particles from an erupting volcano react with oxygen and moisture in the presence of sunlight. Trade winds push it south-west, which is why the Kona coast on the west side gets the most frequent exposure and the sunny side often looks hazy. Prolonged southerly Kona winds can send it the other way, reaching the east side of the island and islands across the state.

Reported symptoms include headaches, watery eyes, sore throat, breathing difficulties including induced asthma attacks, flu-like symptoms and lethargy, and the effects are especially pronounced in children and in people with respiratory conditions. If you use an inhaler, bring it and keep it with you rather than in the room. The Park Service advises checking air quality before a visit.

sections.h2: Three places that are not casual stops
sections.body:
Mauna Kea tops out at 13,803 feet. The Visitor Information Station sits at 9,200 feet and is open 9 a.m. to 9 p.m.; the summit is open from 30 minutes before sunrise to 30 minutes after sunset. Above the station you need four-wheel drive in low range, at least half a tank of fuel, and a vehicle free of invasive species and mud. The station's own guidance is to acclimatise at least 30 minutes there, and that people under 13, pregnant, intoxicated, with high blood pressure or a heart or respiratory condition, or who have scuba dived in the prior 24 hours should not go above it. Around a third of visitors have experienced symptoms of acute altitude sickness.

Waipiʻo Valley Road is currently open to the valley floor only for island residents, county-permitted tour operators, and people practising Native Hawaiian traditional or customary rights. The lookout is open to everyone. Papakōlea Green Sand Beach, about three miles east of Ka Lae, is legally accessible only on foot over rugged paths, with no shade, no drinking water and no facilities.

Hawaiʻi Volcanoes National Park charges $30 per private vehicle, does not accept cash, and is open 24 hours a day, seven days a week.
Only ten Big Island beaches have county lifeguards, on duty 9:30 a.m. to 4:45 p.m. daily.
Non-residents were 53 percent of Hawaiʻi drowning victims in 2013 to 2017, with a fatal ocean drowning rate about eight times the resident rate.
The Mauna Kea summit requires four-wheel drive in low range above the 9,200-foot Visitor Information Station, and around a third of visitors have experienced acute altitude sickness symptoms.
Waipiʻo Valley Road access is limited to residents, county-permitted operators and Native Hawaiian traditional and customary practice; the lookout at the top is open to all.

State Parks warns of dangerous rip currents and pounding shore breaks during periods of high surf at both Hāpuna and Kekaha Kai, and advises that waves over three feet are for experts and all others should stay out of the water and away from the shoreline.
Do not plan a trip around seeing lava. Kīlauea's eruption is episodic, pauses can last weeks, and the eruption area itself is closed to the public.

Altitude on Mauna Kea is a medical risk, not a nuisance. The Visitor Information Station advises that people under 13, pregnant, intoxicated, with high blood pressure or a heart or respiratory condition, or who have scuba dived in the prior 24 hours should not go above it.

title: Big Island Travel Guide: Everything for a First Trip
intro: The Big Island holds 63 percent of the Hawaiian archipelago's land and asks more of a first-time visitor than the other islands do. Two airports two hours apart, a 13,803-foot mountain, an erupting volcano, and a coastline that is mostly unguarded. The trip works when you plan it in regions instead of as one loop. This guide covers when to come, how to move around, and what to know before you get in the water.

sections.body:
The National Weather Service in Honolulu describes two Hawaiian seasons: summer between May and October, and winter between October and April. The warmest months are August and September and the coolest are February and March, not December and January, because ocean temperature lags the sun. Sea surface temperature near Hawaiʻi ranges about six degrees, from a low of 73 or 74 between late February and March to a high near 80 in late September or early October.

On this island the season matters less than the side. Kailua-Kona averaged about 19 inches of rain a year over the 1981 to 2010 period and Hilo airport about 127, so a wet winter forecast usually means the windward side while the Kohala coast stays dry. Snow falls on the Mauna Kea summit in winter.

Humpback whales are in Hawaiian waters in winter, and federal law prohibits approaching within 100 yards in Hawaiʻi, including by boat, kayak, drone, when swimming, or by any other vessel. Plan whale trips for the winter months and everything else around what you want the weather to do.

sections.h2: Which airport, and where to base
sections.body:
Kona International (KOA) is the dry side: Kailua-Kona, the Kohala resorts, the coffee belt, and most of the sandy beaches. Hilo International (ITO) is the green side: waterfalls, gardens, the Hāmākua coast, and a 45-minute drive to Hawaiʻi Volcanoes National Park. They are about 1.5 to 2 hours apart by road.

For one base on a short trip, Kona or the Kohala coast is the more forgiving choice, because that is where the sand and the reliable sun are. For a volcano-focused trip, Hilo or the village of Volcano cuts hours of driving. For a week, split it: a few nights each side.

You need a rental car. Transit exists but does not do what visitors need, and the Park Service notes rideshare is very difficult and sometimes impossible at the volcano, 30 miles from the nearest population centre with drivers. Saddle Road, renamed the Daniel K. Inouye Highway in 2013, is the fast crossing: 52.7 miles, a maximum elevation of 6,632 feet, rebuilt in sections opened in 2007, 2009 and 2013, and now well paved with a separate lane for slower vehicles on the climbs. The old warnings about it are out of date, and rental companies that once prohibited it now generally allow it.

Everything takes longer than it looks. The Park Service puts Kailua-Kona to Hawaiʻi Volcanoes at 95 miles and 2 to 2.5 hours on Highway 11. Coverage is unreliable on Saddle Road, the summit road, Chain of Craters Road and the remoter coasts, so download offline maps. Full numbers are in the driving times guide.

sections.h2: The ocean, read this before you book anything
sections.body:
This is the part first-timers skip. The state Department of Health puts Hawaiʻi's drowning toll at an average of 83 deaths a year including non-residents, with non-residents the majority of victims at 53 percent over 2013 to 2017, and a non-resident fatal ocean drowning rate about eight times the resident rate. The Big Island's non-resident rate is 51.8 per 100,000, third behind Kauaʻi at 82.5 and Maui at 64.6. More Hawaiʻi visitors drown while snorkelling than during any other activity.

Ten beaches on the whole island have county lifeguards, on duty 9:30 a.m. to 4:45 p.m. daily. On the state's list they are Kahaluʻu, White Sands (Laʻaloa), Hāpuna, Spencer, Punaluʻu, Richardson, Carlsmith, Leleiwi, Onekahakaha and Honoliʻi. Everywhere else, including Kua Bay, Makalawena, Hōnaunau and Papakōlea, you are on your own.

The state's ocean safety guidance is short: know your health limits and fitness level, always swim at a lifeguarded beach, learn to swim and snorkel safely, always swim with a buddy, read and obey posted warning signs, and always be aware of the ocean. Two rules matter everywhere here: never swim at a beach where nobody else is in the water, and never turn your back on the ocean on the black-sand and lava-shelf coasts. Check the live page for the beach you are going to on the beaches guide.

Kīlauea has been erupting episodically from Halemaʻumaʻu since December 23, 2024, with more than fifty episodes by mid-2026, separated by pauses of several days or weeks. The eruption area is closed; viewing is from open points along the caldera rim. Entry to Hawaiʻi Volcanoes National Park is $30 per private vehicle for seven days, card only, and the park is open 24 hours a day. Expect closures and delays from a two-year construction project repairing or removing damaged buildings and infrastructure at the summit, and note that parking lots frequently fill by 10 a.m. Do not plan the trip around lava.

Mauna Kea is the other big commitment. The Visitor Information Station sits at 9,200 feet and is open 9 a.m. to 9 p.m.; the summit is open from 30 minutes before sunrise to 30 minutes after sunset. Above the station you need four-wheel drive in low range on unpaved road, half a tank of fuel, and a vehicle free of mud and invasive species, and around a third of visitors have experienced acute altitude sickness symptoms. The station advises acclimatising at least 30 minutes there, and that people under 13, pregnant, intoxicated, with high blood pressure or a heart or respiratory condition, or who have scuba dived in the prior 24 hours should not go above it.

Kona is snorkelling, coffee farms and history: Kahaluʻu, Hōnaunau Bay, and Puʻuhonua o Hōnaunau National Historical Park, $20 per private vehicle with gates open daily 8:15 a.m. until sunset. Kealakekua Bay State Historical Park is free and open 7 a.m. to 8 p.m., but all vessels, including kayaks, canoes, stand-up paddleboards and inflatables, need a State Parks permit to transit the bay, launching from Nāpōʻopoʻo wharf is prohibited, and permitted vessels are prohibited from landing at Kaʻawaloa flat below the Captain Cook Monument.

Kohala is the sand: Hāpuna, Kaunaʻoa, Spencer and Waialea, plus Puʻukoholā Heiau and the towns of Hāwī and Kapaʻau. The Hāmākua coast gives you ʻAkaka Falls, which plunges 442 feet into a stream-eroded gorge on a 0.4-mile paved loop, and the Waipiʻo lookout. Hilo is gardens, museums and the farmers market. Kaʻū is black sand, green sand and Ka Lae, the southernmost point of the United States. The things to do list breaks it down region by region.

State Parks charges non-residents $5 per person plus $10 per vehicle at Hāpuna, ʻAkaka Falls and Kekaha Kai, credit card only. National park fees are separate: $30 per vehicle at Hawaiʻi Volcanoes, $20 per vehicle at Puʻuhonua o Hōnaunau, or $55 for the Hawaiʻi Tri-Park annual pass covering both plus Haleakalā.

Bring a rain shell and a warm layer regardless of the month, because the east side is wet and the high country is cold. Bring mineral sunscreen: Hawaiʻi law makes it unlawful to sell, offer for sale or distribute sunscreen containing oxybenzone or octinoxate without a prescription, effective January 1, 2021. NOAA Fisheries asks you to stay at least 10 feet from sea turtles and 50 feet from Hawaiian monk seals, on land and in the water, and federal law prohibits approaching within 100 yards of humpback whales and within 50 yards of spinner dolphins. Check today's conditions before every swim.

Kailua-Kona averaged about 19 inches of rain a year from 1981 to 2010; Hilo airport averaged about 127.
Hawaiian sea surface temperature runs from 73 or 74 degrees in late February and March to near 80 in late September or early October.
Ten Big Island beaches have county lifeguards, on duty 9:30 a.m. to 4:45 p.m. daily.
Hawaiʻi Volcanoes National Park is $30 per private vehicle for seven days, card only, and open 24 hours a day.
Kīlauea has been erupting episodically from Halemaʻumaʻu since December 23, 2024, with pauses of several days or weeks between episodes.
Mauna Kea's summit is 13,803 feet; the access road is paved only to the 9,200-foot Visitor Information Station.
Federal law prohibits approaching within 100 yards of humpback whales and within 50 yards of spinner dolphins in Hawaiʻi.

title: Things to Do on the Big Island: The Honest Local List
targetQuery: things to do big island hawaii
intro: The Big Island's attractions are spread across 4,028 square miles and several regions that look nothing alike, so the honest answer to what to do here is to pick two regions and do them properly. This is a region-by-region list of what earns the drive, what it costs, and where the ocean risk sits. A fair amount of it is free.

sections.h2: Kona: snorkel, coffee, and the place of refuge
sections.body:
Kahaluʻu Beach Park south of Kailua-Kona is a shallow, reef-protected cove with a county lifeguard, and one of the few places on this coast where you can walk in and see reef straight away. Easy entry is not the same as safe water, so ask the lifeguard about conditions before you get in. Hōnaunau Bay, known as Two Step, has a lava-ledge entry with no sand and no lifeguard, and is described by the island's visitors bureau as a fragile bay for experienced swimmers and snorkelers.

Next door, Puʻuhonua o Hōnaunau National Historical Park is $20 per private vehicle, covering the driver and up to eight passengers, with gates open daily 8:15 a.m. until sunset. Kealakekua Bay State Historical Park is free and open 7 a.m. to 8 p.m., but all vessels, including kayaks, boats, canoes, stand-up paddleboards and inflatables, need a State Parks permit to transit the bay, launching from Nāpōʻopoʻo wharf is prohibited, and permitted vessels are prohibited from landing at Kaʻawaloa flat below the Captain Cook Monument. Two companies hold permits for guided commercial kayak tours to the monument.

Inland, the coffee belt through Holualoa and Captain Cook runs farm tours and tastings. Night snorkel trips to see manta rays operate off the Kona coast and are the signature paid activity here.

sections.h2: Kohala: the sand, and the north end
sections.body:
This is where the white sand is. Hāpuna is the largest white sand beach on the island, has lifeguard services, runs 7:00 a.m. to 7:30 p.m. with gates closing at 8:00 p.m., and charges non-residents $5 per person plus $10 per vehicle. Spencer Beach Park is reef-protected with a county lifeguard. Kaunaʻoa is a crescent of sand leading to calm water, and Waialea has sand and reef. Neither has a lifeguard.

Puʻukoholā Heiau National Historic Site sits next to Spencer: the lava-rock temple built by Kamehameha I, on an easy paved trail. At the far north, Hāwī and Kapaʻau are walkable former plantation towns with galleries, and the road ends at the Pololū Valley lookout. The view from the top costs nothing; the trail down is steep and the beach at the bottom is not a swimming beach.

Waimea is upcountry ranch country, cooler and greener than the coast, with a Saturday farmers market. It is also the junction where you decide between Saddle Road and the Hāmākua route.

ʻAkaka Falls State Park is the reliable stop on the coast: a 0.4-mile paved loop footpath with multiple steps, not wheelchair accessible, past ʻAkaka Falls, which plunges 442 feet into a stream-eroded gorge, with a vista over Kahuna Falls as well. It is open daily 8:30 a.m. to 5:00 p.m., $5 per person plus $10 per vehicle for non-residents, credit card only. The Waipiʻo Valley lookout is open to everyone; road access to the valley floor is currently limited to island residents, county-permitted tour operators, and people practising Native Hawaiian traditional or customary rights.

Hilo is a working town and the place to be when it rains. Liliʻuokalani Gardens is a Japanese garden on the bay. The Pacific Tsunami Museum covers the waves that reshaped the town. The ʻImiloa Astronomy Center connects the Maunakea telescopes to Polynesian navigation. Rainbow Falls is a paved roadside lookout with no hiking involved. The Hilo Farmers Market runs daily, with Wednesday and Saturday the big days.

The Hilo beaches are a different animal from Kona's: reef ponds rather than open sand, and five of the island's ten lifeguarded beaches are here. Richardson fronts the most popular snorkelling site on the east side of the island, and Onekahakaha is a shallow pool with tide pools and inlets. Out in Puna, Lava Tree State Monument is a short shaded loop past lava moulds of trees engulfed by an old flow, and Pohoiki shows what the 2018 Kīlauea eruption did to the coast.

Punaluʻu Black Sand Beach is the island's famous black sand beach and a place where honu, Hawaiian green sea turtles, bask on the shore. It is on the state's lifeguarded list. NOAA Fisheries asks you to stay at least 10 feet from turtles on land and in the water.

Papakōlea Green Sand Beach sits in a bay half circled by Puʻu Mahana, a tuff ring, and its green colour comes from olivine crystals. It is about three miles east of Ka Lae, surrounded by pastureland, and legally accessible only on foot; the paths are rugged from erosion and illegal vehicle traffic, and there is no shade, no drinking water and no facilities. Ka Lae, South Point, is the southernmost point of the United States: wind, cliffs, and no rescue if you go in. Naʻalehu is the practical stop for fuel and food along this stretch.

Hawaiʻi Volcanoes National Park is $30 per private vehicle for seven days, card only, and open 24 hours a day, seven days a week. Kīlauea has been erupting episodically from Halemaʻumaʻu since December 23, 2024, but the eruption area is closed and activity comes in episodes that can be as short as a few hours, separated by pauses of several days or weeks. Plan for the park, not for lava, and expect closures and delays from a two-year construction project at the summit. Parking lots frequently fill by 10 a.m. Kīlauea Iki is the signature hike, down through rainforest onto a solidified lava-lake floor. Devastation Trail is short and paved. Puʻu Loa is a boardwalk over a petroglyph field off Chain of Craters Road, which leads down to the coast and dead-ends there.

Mauna Kea's Visitor Information Station at 9,200 feet is open 9 a.m. to 9 p.m. The summit at 13,803 feet is open from 30 minutes before sunrise to 30 minutes after sunset and requires four-wheel drive in low range on unpaved road, plus half a tank of fuel and a vehicle free of mud and invasive species. If you do not have the right vehicle or the right health profile, the station itself is worth the drive.

Free: every beach on the island except the state parks that charge, the Pololū and Waipiʻo lookouts, the Hilo bayfront and Liliʻuokalani Gardens, Rainbow Falls, the Kailua-Kona farmers market, and the Kohala shoreline trail. Sunset from the Kona side costs nothing.

Rainy: the east side gets most of the rain, so a wet Hilo morning is often a dry Kohala afternoon a couple of hours away. When it is wet everywhere, the museums and gardens in Hilo, the galleries in Hāwī and Holualoa, and a coffee farm tour will fill a day. After heavy rain, stay out of the ocean near stream mouths and harbours, and off wet lava, which is slick.

keyFacts: Hawaiʻi Volcanoes National Park costs $30 per private vehicle for seven days, does not accept cash, and is open 24 hours a day.
Puʻuhonua o Hōnaunau National Historical Park is $20 per private vehicle, with gates open daily 8:15 a.m. until sunset.
ʻAkaka Falls plunges 442 feet into a stream-eroded gorge, on a 0.4-mile paved loop; non-residents pay $5 per person plus $10 per vehicle, credit card only.
All vessels need a State Parks permit to transit Kealakekua Bay, launching from Nāpōʻopoʻo wharf is prohibited, and permitted vessels may not land at Kaʻawaloa flat.
Hāpuna Beach runs 7:00 a.m. to 7:30 p.m. with gates closing at 8:00 p.m., and charges non-residents $5 per person plus $10 per vehicle.
Papakōlea Green Sand Beach lies about three miles east of Ka Lae in a bay half circled by the Puʻu Mahana tuff ring, and is legally accessible only on foot.
The Waipiʻo Valley lookout is open to all; road access to the valley floor is limited to residents, county-permitted operators, and Native Hawaiian traditional and customary practice.
NOAA Fisheries asks visitors to stay at least 10 feet from sea turtles and 50 feet from Hawaiian monk seals, on land and in the water.

title: Big Island Beaches: A Guide to Every Shore (with Live Conditions)
intro: The Big Island is the youngest island in the chain, so it has less sand than the others and what it has is spread thin. White crescents on the Kohala coast, black sand in Kaʻū and Puna, one green-sand cove at the south end, and reef ponds in Hilo. Ten beaches have lifeguards. This guide runs the coast region by region, and every named beach links to its live conditions page.

sections.body:
The Kona side is lava shoreline with pockets of sand. It is the driest coast and the most reliable for snorkelling, and it has only two lifeguarded beaches on the whole stretch.

  • Kahaluʻu Beach Park — shallow reef-protected cove with a county lifeguard, known for honu that frequent its shores. Easy entry is not the same as safe water; ask the lifeguard before you go in.
  • Laʻaloa (Magic Sands / White Sands) — county lifeguard. Also called Disappearing Sands, because the sand strips away in high surf and returns later. Shorebreak here lands directly on sand.
  • Kua Bay (Maniniʻōwali) — white sand in a lava pocket inside Kekaha Kai State Park. State Parks warns of dangerous rip currents and pounding shore breaks during periods of high surf. Non-resident fees of $5 per person plus $10 per vehicle apply to this section as of January 2026.
  • Mahaiʻula — the other Kekaha Kai section, reached by a rough lava road. Picnic tables, no drinking water, no lifeguard services.
  • Makalawena — rough road plus a walk on from Mahaiʻula. No facilities, no drinking water, no lifeguard.
  • Kekaha Kai State Park — daily 8:00 a.m. to 6:30 p.m., gates close at 7:00 p.m. The 4.5-mile Ala Kahakai trail runs north through the park to Kua Bay.
  • Hōnaunau Bay (Two Step) — lava-ledge entry, no beach, good reef, described by the island's visitors bureau as a fragile bay for experienced swimmers and snorkelers. No lifeguard.
  • Kamakahonu (Kailua Pier) — small protected cove beside the pier in town, shallow and sheltered. No lifeguard.

This is where the island's white sand is concentrated, and where the resorts are. It is also open west-facing shoreline that takes a straight hit from swell.

  • Hāpuna Beach — the largest white sand beach on the island, with lifeguard services, open 7:00 a.m. to 7:30 p.m. with gates closing at 8:00 p.m., non-residents $5 per person plus $10 per vehicle. State Parks warns of dangerous rip currents and pounding shore breaks during periods of high surf, and states that waves over three feet are for experts.
  • Kaunaʻoa Beach (Mauna Kea) — a crescent of sand leading to calm water, fronting the hotel, with a limited number of public parking stalls that fill early. No lifeguard.
  • Samuel M. Spencer Beach Park — reef-protected, county lifeguard, next to Puʻukoholā Heiau.
  • Waialea Bay (Beach 69) — sand and reef, snorkelling on calm days, shade from the trees. No lifeguard.
  • Mauʻumae Beach — small and reached on foot along the shoreline trail. No facilities, no lifeguard.
  • Kīholo Bay — spring-fed lagoon, turtles and tidepools between Kona and Kohala. Rough access, brackish and cold water, no lifeguard.
  • Pololū Valley Beach — at the bottom of a steep switchback trail from the lookout at the end of the road. Black sand, strong current, no lifeguard. This is a walking beach, not a swimming one.

The east side works differently. Instead of open sand you get reef ponds, lava benches and river mouths, and five of the island's ten lifeguarded beaches are here. It also rains hard, and heavy rain pushes runoff into the nearshore water.

  • Richardson Ocean Park — the shallow bay fronting Richardson Ocean Center is the most popular snorkelling site on the east side of the island. County lifeguard.
  • Carlsmith Beach Park (Four Mile) — calm reef ponds where turtles graze. County lifeguard.
  • Leleiwi Beach Park (Waiʻuli) — tidepools and ponds, rocky rather than sandy. County lifeguard.
  • Onekahakaha Beach Park — shallow sand-bottomed pool behind a breakwater, with tide pools and inlets. County lifeguard.
  • Honoliʻi Beach Park — the main Hilo surf break, at a river mouth. County lifeguard, strong current, not a casual swimming beach.
  • Pohoiki (Isaac Hale Beach Park) — the 2018 Kīlauea eruption left the pier, boat launch and old protected bay mostly buried under a new black sand beach across Pohoiki Bay, which now impounds geothermal warm-water pools. No lifeguard, rough water.
  • Kehena Beach — black sand at the bottom of a steep, unmaintained trail. No lifeguard, strong current, and no easy way back out of the water.

Kaʻū is the emptiest coast on the island: black sand, green sand, lava benches and a lot of wind. One lifeguarded beach, and long distances between anything.

  • Punaluʻu Black Sand Beach — the island's famous black sand beach and a place to see honu basking on the shore. On the state's lifeguarded list. Cold freshwater springs feed the bay and current runs outside it.
  • Papakōlea Green Sand Beach (Mahana Bay) — olivine sand in a bay half circled by Puʻu Mahana, a tuff ring, about three miles east of Ka Lae. Legally accessible only on foot over rugged eroded paths, with no shade, no drinking water, no facilities and no lifeguard.
  • Ka Lae (South Point) — the southernmost point of the United States. Cliffs, constant wind, no lifeguard, and no easy exit from the water.
  • Whittington Beach Park (Honuʻapo) — old landing ruins and tidepools, for shoreline walking rather than swimming. No lifeguard.
  • Honuʻapo Bay — estuary and tidepools next to Whittington, with birdlife and shoreline walking. Not a swimming spot.
  • Kaʻalualu Bay — remote, reached by a rough track, shoreline and tidepools only. No lifeguard.

sections.h2: Lifeguards, and how few there are
sections.body:
Ten beaches on this island have county lifeguards, on duty Monday to Sunday, 9:30 a.m. to 4:45 p.m. On the state's list they are Kahaluʻu, White Sands (Laʻaloa), Hāpuna, Spencer, Punaluʻu, Richardson, Carlsmith, Leleiwi, Onekahakaha and Honoliʻi. That is ten guarded beaches for 4,028 square miles of island.

The consequence is that most of the beaches people drive furthest to see — Kua Bay, Makalawena, Hōnaunau, Kīholo, Pololū, Papakōlea, Kehena, Pohoiki — have nobody watching. Statewide, the Department of Health records non-residents as the majority of drowning victims at 53 percent, with a non-resident fatal ocean drowning rate about eight times the resident rate, and more visitors drowning while snorkelling than during any other activity. The Big Island's non-resident rate is 51.8 per 100,000, third behind Kauaʻi and Maui. Those facts are connected.

sections.h2: How to choose, and what to check
sections.body:
Match the beach to the people and to the day. For small children, Onekahakaha, Kamakahonu, Spencer and Carlsmith are the shallow, protected options. For snorkelling, go in the morning before the wind builds and stick to Kahaluʻu, Hōnaunau, Richardson or Waialea on a calm day. For scenery without swimming, Pololū, Papakōlea, Ka Lae and Kehena are the ones, and they should stay that way.

The state's own guidance is to know your health limits and fitness level, always swim at a lifeguarded beach, swim with a buddy, read and obey posted warning signs, and always be aware of the ocean. Conditions change by the hour and by the shore. Check the live page for the beach you are going to before you drive out, watch the water for a few minutes before you enter, and ask the lifeguard if there is one. If nobody else is in the water, there is usually a reason. Start from today's conditions.

Hāpuna is the largest white sand beach on the island; it opens 7:00 a.m. to 7:30 p.m. with gates closing at 8:00 p.m., and non-residents pay $5 per person plus $10 per vehicle.

Kekaha Kai State Park opens 8:00 a.m. to 6:30 p.m. with gates closing at 7:00 p.m., has no lifeguard services and no drinking water, and State Parks warns of dangerous rip currents and pounding shore breaks.
Non-resident fees began applying to the Maniniʻōwali (Kua Bay) section of Kekaha Kai as of January 2026.
Papakōlea Green Sand Beach sits about three miles east of Ka Lae and is legally accessible only on foot, over paths made rugged by erosion and illegal vehicle traffic.
The 2018 Kīlauea eruption left Pohoiki's pier, boat launch and old protected bay mostly buried under a new black sand beach that impounds geothermal warm-water pools.
Ka Lae (South Point) is the southernmost point of the United States and has no lifeguard and no easy exit from the water.
